titre: Multidisciplinary Perioperative and Post-Acute Care for Older Adults with Hip Fracture and Cognitive Impairment or Dementia: A Narrative Review.
titre_fr: Multidisciplinary Perioperative and Post-Acute Care for Older Adults with Hip Fracture and Cognitive Impairment or Dementia: A Narrative Review.
auteurs: Han Xinxin, Han Wenzhe, Yin Xuchen, Li Miaomiao
resume: Hip fracture care becomes more complex when an older adult has cognitive impairment. Pain may be expressed behaviorally, consent and goals of care may require supported decision-making, delirium can be difficult to distinguish from baseline impairment, and rehabilitation must accommodate altered learning and communication. Unlike reviews focused predominantly on individual management domains, this narrative review integrates evidence across the entire care pathway, from emergency assessment and perioperative management to inpatient care, post-acute rehabilitation, and discharge planning, with particular emphasis on how cognitive impairment affects care coordination and continuity. The most consistent priorities are timely surgery after correction of reversible instability, reliable recognition and treatment of pain and delirium, early supported activity, and access to rehabilitation adapted to the person's abilities. Cognitive impairment changes how these elements are delivered; it is not, by itself, a reason to withhold them. Decisions about discharge and longer-term recovery are better anchored in prefracture function, transfer ability, residence, caregiver capacity, and the patient's goals than in a cognitive label alone. In advanced dementia, operative and non-operative management are both active care pathways and require explicit discussion of comfort, transfers, nursing burden, survival, and previously expressed values. Direct evidence is most limited for patients with moderate or severe dementia, who are commonly excluded from trials despite being among those most vulnerable to gaps in care.

titre: Esthetic management of gingival lobular capillary hemangioma: A case report.
titre_fr: Esthetic management of gingival lobular capillary hemangioma: A case report.
auteurs: Biswas Debleena, Murugan Thamaraiselvan
resume: Gingival enlargements may manifest with similar presentations, and their management may be particularly challenging in the esthetic zone when surgical removal leads to residual soft-tissue defects that compromise the function and esthetics. This case report describes the management of a lobular capillary hemangioma (LCH) that required a definitive diagnosis, complete surgical excision, and esthetic reconstruction of the gingival and papillary tissues. A 21-year-old woman presented with a progressively enlarging gingival swelling and spacing between the left maxillary anterior teeth. On examination, a soft, nontender, sessile growth was observed, with positive diascopy and palpable pulsations, raising suspicion of a vascular lesion. The lesion was completely excised and submitted for histopathologic examination, which identified it as an LCH. A gingival unit graft (GUG) was simultaneously placed to reconstruct the soft-tissue architecture. The patient healed uneventfully with a satisfactory outcome and soft-tissue graft integration. The case underscores the need for meticulous treatment planning when managing pathological gingival lesions in the esthetic zone. Immediate soft-tissue reconstruction using a GUG following lesion excision may help restore marginal and papillary gingival architecture and achieve favorable functional and esthetic outcomes. Accurate diagnosis of lobular capillary hemangioma requires correlation of clinical findings with histopathologic examination Surgical excision in the esthetic zone should consider the potential loss of marginal and papillary soft tissues Simultaneous gingival unit grafting can help reconstruct gingival and papillary architecture and achieve favorable esthetic outcomes following lesion excision PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: This report presents the management of a gingival lobular capillary hemangioma associated with prominent vascular clinical features and highlights how careful clinical assessment, definitive histopathologic diagnosis, and immediate soft-tissue reconstruction can facilitate favorable functional and esthetic rehabilitation following lesion excision.

titre: Does the Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation Self-Assessment Examination for Residents Predict the Chances of Passing the Part 1 Board Certification Examination? An Update.
titre_fr: Does the Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation Self-Assessment Examination for Residents Predict the Chances of Passing the Part 1 Board Certification Examination? An Update.
auteurs: Lee Samuel J, Tran Victoria M, Tran Duc A, Raddatz Mikaela M, Eickmeyer Sarah M, Nguyen Vu Q
revue: American journal of physical medicine & rehabilitation
resume: Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (PM&R) residents take the Self-Assessment Exam for Residents (SAE-R) offered by the American Academy of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (AAPM&R). The SAE-R is used by residency programs to assess resident knowledge and by residents in preparation for the American Board of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation Certification Examination (ABPMR-CE) Part I. In 2017, Massagli's, "Does the Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation Self-Assessment Examination for Residents Predict the Chances of Passing the Part I Board Certification Examination?", provided data linking performance on the SAE-R with ABPMR-CE Part I passage rate. The objective of this study was to reinvestigate the predictive value of the SAE-R performance on ABPMR-CE Part I with an increased data set from 2015 to 2024. Probability models were developed that predicted passing for PGY-4 SAE-R test takers, in three criterion-referenced score groups: Failing, Just Passing, and Comfortably Passing. The highest Youden Index indicated SAE-R score of 105 as the optimal cut-point and was associated with a 9.2% (95% CI 0.370, 0.465) chance of failing the ABPMR-CE Part I. The SAE-R remains a useful tool in assessing likelihood of passing ABPMR-CE Part I; however, correlations between SAE-R and ABPMR-CE Part I scores were lower than reported previously.

titre: High Use, Low Preparation: A Needs Assessment to Inform Curriculum Development for AI in Residency and Fellowship Training.
titre_fr: High Use, Low Preparation: A Needs Assessment to Inform Curriculum Development for AI in Residency and Fellowship Training.
auteurs: Lin Jing, Oh So Young, Martin Lily, Moroz Alex
revue: American journal of physical medicine & rehabilitation
resume: Generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) has rapidly entered clinical environments, posing a risk of "cognitive offloading" that may impede the development of independent clinical judgment. This study conducted a cross-sectional survey of residents, fellows, and faculty at a large academic medical center in January 2026 to quantify Gen-AI utilization and perceptions in physical medicine and rehabilitation (PM&R) to inform curriculum development. Thirty-six trainees (95% response rate) and 11 faculty members (30% response rate) completed the survey; 43 (91.5%) reported any Gen-AI use and formed the analytic sample. Among users, 72.1% used Gen-AI daily for clinical learning and 51.2% during patient encounters, yet 67.4% were self-taught and only 7.0% always requested citations. Trainees requested citations more often than faculty (P=.048), while faculty more often relied on clinical judgment without additional verification (62.5% vs. 25.7%, P=.089). Gen-AI-derived evidence was rarely surfaced in teaching: 60.5% discussed it during case presentations rarely or never, and only 16.2% always disclosed its origin. Residents are integrating Gen-AI into clinical workflows at rates that outpace faculty familiarity, while verification remains largely undiscussed and untaught. These gaps highlight an urgent need for structured Gen-AI curricula in PM&R residency.

titre: Prevention of Work-Related Musculoskeletal Disorders and Career Sustainability in Head and Neck Reconstructive Surgery: Integrating Ergonomics and Physical Conditioning.
titre_fr: Prevention of Work-Related Musculoskeletal Disorders and Career Sustainability in Head and Neck Reconstructive Surgery: Integrating Ergonomics and Physical Conditioning.
auteurs: Shadgan Babak, Butskiy Oleksandr, Apostolopoulos Nikos C, Sarkissian Lernik, Chang Brent, Anderson Donald
resume: Head and neck reconstructive and plastic surgery exposes surgeons to prolonged static posture, sustained visualization of a narrow operative field, cervical and shoulder loading, fine-motor work, and extended standing. These demands create a substantial occupational musculoskeletal burden. A structured narrative review and expert perspective synthesized evidence from head and neck surgery, reconstructive microsurgery, plastic surgery, surgical ergonomics, occupational health, and rehabilitation. Musculoskeletal symptoms commonly involve the neck, shoulders, back, and upper extremities and often begin during residency. Exposure varies by operative phase, visualization, anthropometric and team-level mismatch, prolonged standing, and repetitive operative workload. Prevention extends beyond ergonomic setup to phase-specific exposure modification, physical conditioning, mobility and recovery, footwear and standing-surface optimization, wearable feedback, early assessment, and diagnosis-specific rehabilitation. Career sustainability requires reducing avoidable occupational load while preserving physical capacity and restoring function through recognition, modification, conditioning, recovery, assessment, and rehabilitation.

titre: Evidence Mapping, Certainty Appraisal, and Acupoint Prescription Pattern Mining of Acupuncture for Poststroke Dysphagia: An Overview of Systematic Reviews.
titre_fr: Evidence Mapping, Certainty Appraisal, and Acupoint Prescription Pattern Mining of Acupuncture for Poststroke Dysphagia: An Overview of Systematic Reviews.
auteurs: Lan Guohao, Wu Minmin, Zhang Jiongliang, Li Yuxuan, Wang Yuting, Su Yumeng, Dong Zhiliang, Wei Xiangyu, Zhu Luwen
resume: To characterize the methodological quality, certainty of evidence, primary-study overlap, outcome coverage, and recurrent acupuncture prescription patterns in the existing secondary evidence on acupuncture for poststroke dysphagia (PSD). Systematic reviews and meta-analyses (SRs/MAs) evaluating acupuncture for PSD were identified. Methodological quality was assessed using A Measurement Tool to Assess Systematic Reviews 2 (AMSTAR 2), certainty of evidence using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach, and primary-study overlap using the corrected covered area (CCA). Evidence mapping summarized outcome coverage and certainty, and prescription pattern mining explored frequently used acupoints and combinations. Forty-five SRs/MAs were included. Under the original AMSTAR 2 critical-domain configuration, one review was rated moderate, eight low, and 36 critically low. GRADE indicated that most outcome evidence was of low or very low certainty. The CCA was 0.34%, indicating slight overlap of primary studies across reviews. Evidence was concentrated on total effective rate and swallowing-function outcomes, whereas patient-important outcomes, including aspiration/pneumonia, nutritional status, safety, and quality of life, were underrepresented. Frequently used acupoints included Fengchi (GB20), Lianquan (RN23), Jinjin (EX-HN12), and Yuye (EX-HN13), with recurrent combinations reflecting local stimulation and swallowing-related functional regulation. Current secondary evidence suggests that acupuncture, primarily as an adjunctive intervention, may improve swallowing-related outcomes in PSD, but confidence remains limited by methodological weaknesses and low certainty of evidence. Future studies should improve methodological rigor, standardize clinically important outcomes, and prospectively validate recurrent prescription patterns.

titre: Beyond Mass Movement: Decoding Functional Recruitment Saturation and Neuromuscular Dominance in Facial Synkinesis via Dynamic Surface EMG.
titre_fr: Beyond Mass Movement: Decoding Functional Recruitment Saturation and Neuromuscular Dominance in Facial Synkinesis via Dynamic Surface EMG.
auteurs: Lee Ji Hae, Kim Dae Rock, Kim Jin Han, Park Ji Seong, Kim Woo Shik, Kim Jin
resume: Facial synkinesis is traditionally viewed as a generalized "mass-movement" phenomenon. However, the physiological mechanism behind why increased voluntary effort paradoxically worsens symmetry remains poorly understood. We aimed to quantify dynamic neuromuscular remodeling and identify objective predictors of patient-reported distress using multi-channel dynamic surface electromyography (dsEMG). Fifty-three patients with post-paralytic facial synkinesis (mean age, 51.57 ± 13.11 years) following peripheral facial nerve paralysis were evaluated between March 2025 and August 2025. The study followed the STROBE guidelines. A five-channel dsEMG protocol was used to assess the Frontalis, Orbicularis Oculi, Zygomaticus Major, Depressor Anguli Oris, and Platysma. We calculated the Recruitment Expansion Ratio (RER; peak/mean amplitude) and the Lip Amplitude Ratio (upper-lip elevator/lower-lip depressor). These metrics were correlated with the Synkinesis Assessment Questionnaire (SAQ) to identify hierarchical predictors of patient distress. A significant "Weak Smile Paradox" was observed; Lip Amplitude Ratios were relatively preserved during submaximal effort but collapsed toward lower-lip dominance during maximal effort. This was driven by a profound depletion of the RER in affected elevators (1.38 vs. 2.64 on the normal side, p < 0.001), indicating "Functional Saturation." Affected-side Lower Lip Dominance showed the strongest correlation with SAQ scores (r = -0.492, p = 0.0013), far outweighing Pathological Co-activation intensity or patient age. Facial synkinesis is characterized by a "recruitment ceiling" in mid-facial elevators, where excess neural drive is diverted into synkinetic pathways. The ΔLip Ratio and functional saturation are critical determinants of recovery. These findings advocate for a paradigm shift from muscle strengthening to efficiency-based rehabilitation and provide a electrophysiological roadmap for precision chemodenervation and selective neurectomy.

titre: Learned helplessness is associated with jump-landing biomechanics following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
titre_fr: Learned helplessness is associated with jump-landing biomechanics following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
auteurs: Burland Julie P, Lepley Adam S, Lepley Lindsey K
resume: Persistent biomechanical alterations following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) contribute to reduced functional performance, increased reinjury risk, and diminished joint health. Rehabilitation emphasizes strength and functional restoration; however, neurobehavioral adaptations may persist. Learned helplessness, characterized by reduced motivation, maladaptive biomechanics, and learned non-use of the reconstructed limb, may relate to post-operative neuromuscular control. However, its relationship with dynamic movement after ACLR remains unclear. This study examined the association between learned helplessness and bilateral lower extremity kinematics during jump-landings in individuals following ACLR. Thirty-three individuals with primary, unilateral ACLR completed a learned helplessness scale and jump-landing task with three-dimensional lower-extremity kinematics. Sagittal and frontal plane knee and hip angles were assessed at initial contact and peak landing. Correlations and regression analyses examined associations with learned helplessness, controlling for age, sex, and time since surgery. Participants were 2.78 ± 2.78 years post-ACLR and demonstrated low helplessness scores. Greater learned helplessness was moderately associated with greater peak knee abduction in the ACLR limb (r = 0.564, p = 0.001). Weak associations were also observed with reduced peak hip flexion in the ACLR (r = -0.370, p = 0.048) and contralateral limbs (r = -0.415, p = 0.025), which did not survive sensitivity analyses. Learned helplessness was independently associated with greater peak knee abduction angle in the ACLR limb (B = 0.230, p = 0.007). The overall model accounted for 34.8% of the variance in peak knee abduction. Learned helplessness appears to be associated with frontal plane knee mechanics following ACLR. Consideration of psychological and neurobehavioral constructs in rehabilitation and return-to-sport assessment following ACLR is important.

titre: [Introduction of a next-generation "smart" cochlear implant (Cochlear™ Nucleus® Nexa™) in Hungary: our early experiences].
titre_fr: [Introduction of a next-generation "smart" cochlear implant (Cochlear™ Nucleus® Nexa™) in Hungary: our early experiences].
auteurs: Posta Bálint, Nagy Roland, Perényi Ádám, Csanády Miklós, Jarabin János, Ivaskó Lívia, Molnár Fiona, Perényi-Csáthi Éva, Bere Zsófia, Rovó László
resume: The first cochlear implantation at the Department of Oto-Rhino-Laryngology and Head and Neck Surgery, Albert Szent-Györgyi Medical School, University of Szeged, was performed in 1995. Since then, 1077 implantations have been carried out at our institution. On 25-26 June 2025, we performed the first Hungarian implantations of the Cochlear™ Nucleus® Nexa™ system at our department. The manufacturer presents this device as the world's first "smart" cochlear implant. The aim of our study was to summarize the early experience with Nexa™ implantations in Hungary, which may represent a new milestone in modern cochlear implant technology. Two patients with sensorineural hearing loss - an 11-year-old child and a 56-year-old woman - underwent left-sided cochlear implantation with the new implant system. Both procedures were performed through a standard transmastoid approach, followed by posterior tympanotomy and round-window access. Intraoperative electrophysiological measurements, including impedance testing, transimpedance matrix measurement, electrically evoked stapedius reflex threshold measurement and neural response telemetry, were used for device and electrode function assessment. Both operations were completed without complications. Intraoperative measurements confirmed appropriate implant function, and the postoperative course was uneventful in both patients. Initial activation and fitting of the external sound processor followed a workflow similar to that used with previous systems, supplemented by programming of the implanted electronics. Initial programming and fitting were completed without technical difficulties in both cases, and the early audiological experience was favorable. The novelty of the Nexa™ system lies in the future upgradeability of the internal unit, implant-level data management, and new technological solutions supporting intraoperative monitoring and long-term care. Based on our initial experience, the implant system can be safely integrated into established surgical and audiological workflows. The first Hungarian use of the Nexa™ system may represent an important technological advance in cochlear implant care in Hungary. Its upgradeable architecture may allow recipients to benefit from future technological developments. Orv Hetil. 2026; 167(44): 1778-1784.

titre: Mapping the gap between lab and life: A scoping review of proprioceptive assessment technologies (2016-2025) using the Ecological Validity and Technological Maturity Indices.
titre_fr: Mapping the gap between lab and life: A scoping review of proprioceptive assessment technologies (2016-2025) using the Ecological Validity and Technological Maturity Indices.
auteurs: Lyu Mengde, Pranata Adrian, Farragher Joshua, Adams Roger, Xue Xiao'ao, Qian Huaibin, Huang Jinglei, Shao Xuerong, Wang Xueying, Chang Lin, Kang Ming, Zhang Tongzhou, Luan Lijiang, Deng Fawei, Shi Xiaojian, Han Jia, Pappas Evangelos
revue: Journal of sport and health science
resume: Proprioception is fundamental to motor control, athletic performance, and rehabilitation. Over the past decade, proprioceptive assessment has undergone substantial methodological developments. However, whether recent innovations have improved both measurement precision and ecological validity remains unclear. This scoping review examined methodological developments in proprioceptive assessment from 2016 to 2025 across 3 core paradigms: joint position reproduction, threshold to detection of passive motion, and active movement extent discrimination assessment. Web of Science, PubMed, Embase, and Scopus were systematically searched for peer-reviewed studies introducing novel proprioceptive assessment methods published between 2016 and 2025. Fifty-six studies met the inclusion criteria. To support structured comparison, we developed 2 novel metrics: the Ecological Validity Index (7-point scale) and the Technological Maturity Index (4-point scale). Studies were analyzed according to technological modality, task design, and psychometric properties and then were scored on both indices. Measurement capability and reproducibility were evaluated indirectly through reported technical specifications and reliability metrics. The 56 included studies revealed 2 methodological orientations: technology-driven approaches (n = 42) and task-driven approaches (n = 14). Joint position reproduction was the most frequently represented paradigm (n = 41), followed by active movement extent discrimination assessment (n = 12) and threshold to detection of passive motion (n = 5). Moderate ecological validity was most common (n = 29), followed by low (n = 21) and high ecological validity (n = 6). Technological maturity was predominantly moderate (n = 52), and no study simultaneously achieved both high ecological validity and high technological maturity. At the paradigm level, active movement extent discrimination assessment showed the highest mean ecological validity score. At the technology level, physical apparatuses and props showed the highest ecological validity, whereas portable digital devices showed the highest technological maturity. Psychometric reporting varied substantially, and absolute reliability metrics were underreported. Contemporary proprioceptive assessment methods have developed along 2 major pathways: technology-driven and task-driven approaches. Although recent innovations have improved measurement capability, ecological validity remains insufficiently addressed, and a gap persists between laboratory-based precision and functionally relevant assessment. Future progress will depend on better integrating these 2 pathways to support more ecologically relevant, technically mature, and clinically useful proprioceptive assessment systems.

titre: Hand-Arm Bimanual Intensive Therapy Including Lower Extremities (HABIT-ILE) in adults with chronic stroke: a randomized controlled trial.
titre_fr: Hand-Arm Bimanual Intensive Therapy Including Lower Extremities (HABIT-ILE) in adults with chronic stroke: a randomized controlled trial.
auteurs: Gathy Estelle, Ebner-Karestinos Daniela, Carton de Tournai Astrid, Herman Enimie, Araneda Rodrigo, Rosselli Zélie, Somville Merlin, Dricot Laurence, Macq Benoît, Vandermeeren Yves, Bleyenheuft Yannick
revue: Annals of physical and rehabilitation medicine
resume: Stroke rehabilitation guidelines recommend goal-oriented, task-specific, intensive interventions. Yet most programs emphasize upper extremity (UE) recovery, overlooking lower extremities (LEs) and trunk, which are essential for activities of daily living. Consequently, Hand-Arm Bimanual Intensive Therapy Including LEs (HABIT-ILE) represents a promising approach for stroke rehabilitation. This randomized controlled trial aimed to determine the effect of HABIT-ILE and to compare its efficacy with a control group in adults with chronic hemiparetic stroke by promoting greater improvements across the body functions, activity, and participation domains of the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health. Forty-six adults with hemiparetic chronic stroke were randomized to either a 2-week (50 h, 5 h/day) HABIT-ILE camp-setting program in Brussels, Belgium, or to continue their usual neurorehabilitation (mean = 4 h 36 min) for over the same period. Participants were assessed before, immediately, and at 3 months after intervention using the Adult Assisting Hand Assessment Stroke (Ad-AHA Stroke, primary outcome), the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM), the Fugl Meyer Assessment for UEs (FMA-UE), the Wolf Motor Function Test (WMFT), the ABILHAND-CS and ACTIVLIM-CS questionnaires, the six-minute walk test, the modified Rankin Scale and the Stroke Impact Scale (SIS). The ANCOVA revealed a significant between-groups difference favoring the HABIT-ILE group (TG), with a time effect observed for the Ad-AHA Stroke (TG: at 2 weeks = +6.24% of logits; at 3 months = +7.05% of logits), WMFT (Functional Ability Scale, all P ≤ 0.041), and COPM (P < 0.001, performance and satisfaction) at both 2 weeks and 3 months. We found a similar significant effect for the SIS (hand function, P = 0.003) at 2 weeks and the FMA-UE and ABILHAND-CS at 3 months (all P ≤ 0.033). We observed no significant between-group differences for the other outcomes, including LEs measures. In adults with chronic stroke, HABIT-ILE intervention significantly improved spontaneous bimanual use, motor function, and ability of the paretic UE (both externally rated and self-perceived) and reduced participation restrictions compared with the control group. This randomized controlled trial was registered on December 11th, 2020, on ClinicalTrials.gov as "HABIT-ILE in Adults With Chronic Stroke (HABIT-ILE Stroke)", with the registration number NCT04664673 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04664673?cond=NCT04664673&rank=).

titre: TMJ Dislocation in Dependent Older Adults in PA/LTC: A Recognition-to-Maintenance Framework.
titre_fr: TMJ Dislocation in Dependent Older Adults in PA/LTC: A Recognition-to-Maintenance Framework.
auteurs: Choi Eunhye
revue: Journal of the American Medical Directors Association
resume: To reframe temporomandibular joint dislocation as a potentially reversible oral-function emergency in post-acute and long-term care (PA/LTC) and propose a recognition-to-maintenance framework for older adults unable to reliably report symptoms. Problem-based narrative review and commentary, illustrated by deidentified composite vignettes. Older adults in PA/LTC, rehabilitation, nursing home, and LTC hospital settings, particularly those with communication impairment, neurologic disease, frailty, edentulism, denture use, enteral feeding, or recent airway manipulation. PubMed was searched from inception, with the search updated on September 8, 2026, using 3 complementary strategies (755 records; 466 unique after deduplication). The updated search results were reviewed for relevance against predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, and clinically informative sources meeting these criteria were incorporated into the narrative synthesis to identify PA/LTC recognition and maintenance gaps. Available evidence, consisting mainly of reviews, retrospective series, and case reports, suggests 3 PA/LTC-relevant vulnerabilities: presentation that is silent or absorbed into neurologic or frailty-related explanations, uncertain onset, and failure to verify maintained reduction or detect recurrence. During neurologic workup, dysarthria, drooling, facial asymmetry, feeding decline, and apparent dysphagia may trigger stroke-oriented assessment while mouth closure may not be deliberately assessed, and dislocation may both mimic and be mimicked by dystonic conditions. The proposed "last-known-normal jaw closure" question is intended as a practical bedside prompt, not a validated triage metric. In PA/LTC, temporomandibular joint dislocation should be approached as a recognition-to-maintenance problem. Same-day assessment of oral-function change, avoidance of repeated forceful attempts, maintained-reduction verification, and caregiver-facing recurrence surveillance warrant validation.

titre: Early functional deterioration during first-line ICI-based therapy in advanced NSCLC: implications for supportive care.
titre_fr: Early functional deterioration during first-line ICI-based therapy in advanced NSCLC: implications for supportive care.
auteurs: Lekka Christiana, Chynkiamis Nikolaos, Vontetsianos Angelos, Anagnostopoulou Christina, Zamarias Vassilios, Kotsakis Athanasios, Syrigos Konstantinos, Saloustros Emmanouil
revue: Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer
resume: To compare objective functional measures for identifying early functional deterioration during first-line ICI-based therapy in advanced NSCLC and explore their relevance for supportive-care monitoring. This secondary exploratory analysis used prospectively collected data from a randomized trial of pulmonary rehabilitation. Forty-two participants with baseline and 8-week assessments were evaluated using quadriceps force, SPPB, and 6MWD. Early deterioration was defined as decline in at least one domain. Deterioration frequency, cross-domain agreement, baseline associations, and subsequent PFS were examined, accounting for randomized treatment allocation. Under the primary operational definitions, deterioration in at least one functional domain occurred in 29/42 participants (69.0%) despite stable ECOG performance status. Deterioration affected quadriceps force in 23 (54.8%), SPPB in 14 (33.3%), and 6MWD in 5 (11.9%); 16 participants deteriorated in one domain and 13 in two. Frequencies differed significantly across measures (Cochran's Q=16.76, p<0.001), with low pairwise agreement. No examined baseline characteristic was significantly associated with deterioration after adjustment for PR/UC allocation. Participants with deterioration had numerically less favorable subsequent PFS, but the association was not statistically significant. Early functional deterioration during first-line ICI-based therapy was common and heterogeneous across domains. Repeated objective assessment across complementary functional measures may help identify emerging functional vulnerability and support timely individualized supportive-care evaluation.

titre: Clinical Practice Patterns of Orthoptists in Post-Stroke Vision Care in Australia.
titre_fr: Clinical Practice Patterns of Orthoptists in Post-Stroke Vision Care in Australia.
auteurs: Koklanis Konstandina, Vukicevic Meri, Eng Marc Hseun-Qi
revue: The British and Irish orthoptic journal
resume: Vision impairment is common after stroke and whilst orthoptists are well placed to assess and manage post-stroke visual deficits, their role within Australian stroke care pathways is poorly understood. This study examined orthoptic practice patterns and perceived barriers to post-stroke vision care in Australia. A cross-sectional online survey of practising Australian orthoptists working in stroke care was conducted, collecting data on demographics, practice settings, referral pathways, assessment and management practices, and perceived barriers. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively, and open-ended responses thematically. Twenty-nine orthoptists completed the survey, representing an estimated 22% of the orthoptic workforce engaged in stroke care. Respondents were mainly experienced clinicians working in private ophthalmology or hospital outpatient eye clinics, with limited involvement in stroke units or rehabilitation settings. Orthoptists reported managing a broad range of post-stroke visual deficits, reflected in comprehensive visual assessments and rehabilitation strategies. Orthoptic involvement most often commenced months post-stroke and key barriers to orthoptic services included limited awareness of orthoptic roles, exclusion from multidisciplinary stroke teams, funding and lack of guideline inclusion. Post-stroke vision care in Australia broadly aligns with international practice, but survey findings suggest that the timing and context of orthoptic involvement may be influenced by structural and organisational factors.

titre: YouTube Videos on Arthrogenic Muscle Inhibition Show Low-to-Moderate Quality and Reliability.
titre_fr: YouTube Videos on Arthrogenic Muscle Inhibition Show Low-to-Moderate Quality and Reliability.
auteurs: Conteduca Jacopo, Longo Damiano, Piacquadio Fabrizio, Casto Alberto, Valentino Luigi, Bernetti Andrea, Rollo Giuseppe
resume: To evaluate the quality and reliability of YouTube videos on arthrogenic muscle inhibition (AMI) using validated assessment instruments and to identify predictors of higher-quality content. This cross-sectional study analyzed English-language YouTube videos identified on November 2, 2025, using the search terms "arthrogenic muscle inhibition" and "AMI." Video quality was assessed using the DISCERN, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Global Quality Score instruments. Assessments were performed independently by 2 experienced knee surgeons. Correlations between quality scores and video characteristics (views, likes, comments, time online, duration, source, and topic) were analyzed using nonparametric tests and multivariate regression with Bonferroni correction. A total of 45 videos were analyzed. Mean scores were 44.9 ± 20.5 for DISCERN, 1.47 ± 1.56 for Journal of the American Medical Association, and 2.93 ± 1.53 for Global Quality Score, indicating overall low-to-moderate quality. Video quality was strongly correlated across scoring systems (ρ > 0.86, P < .001). Videos addressing mechanisms and therapeutic interventions had the highest quality (mean DISCERN score: 62.7), whereas videos on patient experience and rehabilitation alone scored lowest (P < .001). Comment count correlated negatively with DISCERN scores (ρ = -0.37, P = .046). Video topic was the strongest independent predictor of video quality (P < .001). YouTube videos on AMI demonstrate low-to-moderate quality and reliability, with substantial variation by topic and content type. Improving the quality of online AMI-related content may enhance patient education and promote accurate dissemination of rehabilitation information.

titre: A technical review of dynamic brain functional imaging combined with EEG spectral parameters in the screening of early-stage brain injury.
titre_fr: A technical review of dynamic brain functional imaging combined with EEG spectral parameters in the screening of early-stage brain injury.
auteurs: Ruan Hongmei, Liao Liqing, Zhang Yuan, Liu Zicai, Wu Qiang
resume: Early-stage brain injury encompasses subtypes such as mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), silent stroke and subclinical brain injury. It is characterised by negative imaging findings, subtle symptoms and a high risk of long-term neurological deficits, presenting a key challenge in the early screening and prevention of neurological diseases. Traditional imaging techniques, such as structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Computed Tomography (CT), can only identify organic morphological lesions. Their detection rate for early micro-injuries at the level of neuronal electrophysiology and brain network function is extremely low. Consequently, these techniques struggle to meet the clinical needs for early screening, assessment, and intervention. Electroencephalography (EEG) spectral changes (including conventional spectral slowing and 1/f aperiodic abnormalities) and large-scale dynamic neural network disruption across the entire brain are core pathological features of early brain functional damage; they may serve as indirect correlates of microscopic pathological changes such as an imbalance in neuronal excitation-inhibition and abnormalities in the efficiency of brain information transmission. Based on this, this paper proposes a Dynamic-Spectral Coupling (DSC) framework, which proposes spectral abnormalities as a potential upstream mechanism associated with network reorganisation. Within this framework, this narrative review summarizes dynamic functional magnetic resonance imaging (dynamic fMRI), EEG spectral analysis and multimodal fusion technologies, with a particular focus on elucidating the coupling mechanisms between EEG periodic and 1/f aperiodic spectral parameters and dynamic brain network indicators. The review outlines the screening value and application advantages of multimodal fusion technologies in mTBI, occult cerebrovascular injury and subclinical brain injury. Furthermore, the paper summarises the current limitations of these technologies in terms of clinical translation, methodology and database development. Taking into account the clinical needs of neurorehabilitation, it proposes future development directions, including the development of lightweight devices, AI-assisted diagnosis, the establishment of standardised analytical systems and the translation of precision rehabilitation. The aim is to provide technical guidance and theoretical support for screening, risk stratification and rehabilitation planning in early-stage brain injury, while acknowledging that clinical utility remains to be established.

titre: Airflow-enabled swallowing rehabilitation after tracheostomy in acquired neurological disease: mechanisms, current evidence, and a stage-based clinical pathway.
titre_fr: Airflow-enabled swallowing rehabilitation after tracheostomy in acquired neurological disease: mechanisms, current evidence, and a stage-based clinical pathway.
auteurs: Xia Jiayi, Pei Song, Qin Hongwei, Lu Yao, Zhou Song, Bai Yulong
resume: Tracheostomy is common after severe stroke and other acquired neurological diseases, yet the route from airway stabilization to safe oral feeding and decannulation is often fragmented. Dysphagia in this setting cannot be attributed to the tracheostomy tube alone: neurological injury, prolonged intubation, deconditioning, impaired alertness, and laryngeal injury interact with upper-airway bypass. Nevertheless, loss of expiratory airflow through the larynx and reduction of subglottic pressure may weaken sensory input, respiratory-swallow coordination, cough effectiveness, and secretion clearance. This Mini Review examines airflow-restoration strategies as a way to reconnect this aerodigestive sensorimotor loop. Cuff deflation, tube occlusion, one-way speaking valves, above-cuff airflow, and pulsed subglottic air or oxygen share a physiological aim but differ in airway requirements, dose control, and safety. Small mechanistic studies and recent clinical trials suggest improvements in penetration-aspiration, residue, spontaneous swallowing, and secretion management; however, the evidence remains heterogeneous, and oxygen has not been separated from the mechanical effects of flow and pressure. We therefore propose that airflow should be used as phenotype-guided sensory priming immediately before or during task-specific feeding, rather than treated as an isolated device intervention. A stage-based pathway links instrumental assessment, airflow restoration, functional eating practice, and decannulation readiness. Future trials should report gas composition, flow, pressure, pulse timing, humidity, cuff condition, and concurrent feeding tasks, and should prioritize oral intake, pneumonia, and decannulation alongside physiological outcomes.

titre: Comparative efficacy of brain-computer interface training with different feedback modalities for post-stroke upper-limb motor recovery: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
titre_fr: Comparative efficacy of brain-computer interface training with different feedback modalities for post-stroke upper-limb motor recovery: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
auteurs: Wang Fuqiang, Lu Xiao, Deng Yunhong, Li Yaojiang, Li Xiaodi, Huang Congping, Ma Mengliang, He Bianhong, Yu Lang, Deng Lixia
resume: Brain-computer interface (BCI) training may improve post-stroke upper-limb recovery through closed-loop feedback, but the comparative efficacy of different feedback modalities remains uncertain. This study compared BCI training with different feedback modalities for post-stroke upper-limb motor impairment. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and Scopus were searched from inception through April 2026 for randomized controlled trials of BCI-based upper-limb rehabilitation after stroke. BCI interventions were classified by feedback modality and feedback contingency into multimodal feedback (BCI-MM), robotic or exoskeleton-assisted feedback (BCI-Robot), functional electrical stimulation feedback (BCI-FES), and visual feedback (BCI-visual), while comparator interventions were classified separately, with usual rehabilitation (UR) as the reference. Random-effects network meta-analysis estimated WMDs with 95% CIs. The primary outcome was Fugl-Meyer Assessment for Upper Extremity (FMA-UE); secondary outcomes were the Action Research Arm Test (ARAT) and Wolf Motor Function Test (WMFT). Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool, and certainty was assessed using CINeMA. Twenty-two trials involving 956 patients across subacute, chronic, and mixed post-stroke stages were included. The FMA-UE network contained 11 connected nodes, with no global or local inconsistency. Compared with UR, BCI-Robot showed greater FMA-UE improvement (WMD = 6.28, 95% CI 2.70-9.86), as did non-BCI robotic training (WMD = 4.26, 95% CI 0.42-8.10) and BCI-MM (WMD = 4.03, 95% CI 1.00-7.06). BCI-FES did not differ significantly from UR. BCI-visual had the highest SUCRA value (77.6%), but its comparison with UR was non-significant, with very low certainty of evidence; no BCI feedback modality was superior to another. Secondary outcomes showed greater ARAT improvement with BCI-Robot versus UR, whereas WMFT findings were non-significant. Certainty for the main FMA-UE comparisons was low or very low. BCI-Robot and BCI-MM showed statistically significant FMA-UE benefits versus UR, although certainty was low. As non-BCI robotic training also showed benefit, the BCI-Robot effect cannot be attributed to BCI alone. No BCI feedback modality was statistically superior to another. Further high-quality direct-comparison trials are needed. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261370474, Unique Identifier: CRD420261370474.

titre: Effects of wearable lower-limb robotic exoskeleton-assisted gait training on balance, walking, and activities of daily living after stroke: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
titre_fr: Effects of wearable lower-limb robotic exoskeleton-assisted gait training on balance, walking, and activities of daily living after stroke: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
auteurs: Zhang Zezhong, Zhang Xinyuan, Mao Sujie, Cao Lei, Wang Zilong, Wu Jingtao, Zang Wanli
resume: Wearable lower-limb robotic exoskeleton-assisted gait training encompasses heterogeneous overground and treadmill/platform-based implementations. Comparative effects remain uncertain. We synthesised evidence from randomised controlled trials (RCTs) on walking, balance, lower-limb motor function, and activities of daily living (ADL). We searched PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science Core Collection, and China National Knowledge Infrastructure from inception to February 26, 2026. We included RCTs comparing wearable lower-limb robotic exoskeleton-assisted gait training (overground and/or treadmill/platform-based) with usual rehabilitation or other controls. Effects were pooled using random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation and Hartung-Knapp adjustment; 95% prediction intervals were reported when applicable. Certainty was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach, and publication bias was evaluated for outcomes with ≥10 studies. Fourteen RCTs (n = 565) were included. Pooled between-group estimates favoured intervention groups for walking independence measured by the Functional Ambulation Category (FAC; mean difference [MD] = 0.39, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.15-0.63), balance measured by the Berg Balance Scale (BBS; MD = 1.66, 95% CI 0.52-2.81), and lower-limb motor function measured by the Fugl-Meyer Assessment of the Lower Extremity (FMA-LE; MD = 2.40, 95% CI 1.63-3.16). The 6-Minute Walk Test estimate favoured intervention groups (MD = 19.83, 95% CI 2.21-37.45), although its prediction interval crossed the null. No between-group differences emerged for walking speed, mobility, or ADL. Certainty was moderate for FAC, BBS, and FMA-LE and low to very low for other outcomes. No small-study effects were detected for BBS (k = 11; p > 0.05). Across heterogeneous exoskeleton-assisted gait-training interventions, pooled estimates favoured intervention groups for walking independence, balance, and lower-limb motor function. However, most prediction intervals crossed the null, certainty for other outcomes was low to very low, and inconsistent reporting limited analyses of training environment and precluded granular analyses of body-weight support, assistance strategy, patient engagement, comparator content, dose, and patient selection. These estimates reflect heterogeneous intervention-comparator packages and cannot determine whether differences are attributable to the robotic device category itself or support specific prescribing recommendations. Larger, stratified RCTs with standardised reporting and longer follow-up are needed to identify influential intervention and patient characteristics. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261327255.

titre: Robot-assisted training for post-stroke lower-limb dysfunction: an umbrella review.
titre_fr: Robot-assisted training for post-stroke lower-limb dysfunction: an umbrella review.
auteurs: Wang Lei, Wang Can, Cao Qian, Yin Keping, Ding Lingnan, Chen Ailian
resume: This study aimed to reappraise published systematic reviews and meta-analyses on robot-assisted training for lower-limb motor dysfunction after stroke and evaluate their methodological quality, reporting completeness, and certainty of evidence. Seven databases were searched, including CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, PubMed, Cochrane Library, Embase, and Web of Science, from inception to January 15, 2026. Eligible studies were systematic reviews or meta-analyses that were based on randomized controlled trials. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and quality appraisal. The methodological quality of the included reviews was assessed using A MeaSurement Tool to Assess systematic Reviews (AMSTAR) 2, and the reporting of this umbrella review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Overviews of Reviews (PRIOR) guideline. The reporting completeness of the included systematic reviews and meta-analyses was evaluated using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 checklist. The certainty of evidence was graded using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. Nineteen reviews were included, comprising eight Chinese and 11 English publications. Primary-study overlap across reviews was moderate (CCA = 7.44%). According to AMSTAR 2, three reviews were rated as high quality, six as moderate quality, six as low quality, and four as critically low quality. PRISMA completeness scores ranged from 14.5 to 23.5 out of a maximum possible score of 27. Among the 70 extracted outcomes, none was rated as high-certainty evidence, 20 were of moderate certainty, 32 were of low certainty, and 18 were of very low certainty. Overall, robot-assisted training showed potential benefits for balance and lower-extremity motor function, whereas evidence for walking-related outcomes remained less consistent. Evidence was most consistent for balance and lower-extremity motor impairment, whereas findings for walking independence, endurance, functional mobility, and gait speed were less consistent and generally supported by low-to-moderate certainty evidence. More rigorously designed primary trials and better-conducted systematic reviews are needed. The review protocol was registered under Prospero, https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/home (Registration No: CRD420261419692).

titre: Direct alcohol biomarkers in alcohol use disorder rehabilitation: Analytical challenges, longitudinal interpretation, and clinical utility.
titre_fr: Direct alcohol biomarkers in alcohol use disorder rehabilitation: Analytical challenges, longitudinal interpretation, and clinical utility.
auteurs: Turaev Bobir, Sultanov Shokhrukh, Sharapova Dilfuza, Azizova Feruza, Shaumarov Azizkhon, Gulamova Gulshan, Khafizova Dilnoza
revue: Clinica chimica acta; international journal of clinical chemistry
resume: Direct alcohol biomarkers can strengthen monitoring during alcohol use disorder rehabilitation, but their clinical value depends on the question being asked, specimen quality, and interpretation over time. This critical narrative review examines phosphatidylethanol (PEth) in blood and ethyl glucuronide and ethyl sulfate in urine, with hair ethyl glucuronide considered as a complementary retrospective measure. Targeted literature searches and reference tracing identified analytical investigations, longitudinal treatment studies, consensus documents, and trials incorporating biomarker feedback. Study designs were appraised with explicit descriptors of evidence strength. PEth offers an extended observation window, whereas urinary metabolites are better suited to investigating more recent exposure. Neither a single concentration nor a fixed detection window reliably reconstructs drinking behavior. Residual PEth after cessation, erythrocyte turnover, transfusion, post-collection formation, urine dilution, renal dysfunction, and laboratory differences can materially affect interpretation. PEth harmonization cannot be assumed and external quality assessment is limited. Serial measurements anchored to baseline, collection dates, and temporally matched self-report are therefore more informative than isolated positive or negative classifications. Trials of biomarker-supported contingency management provide evidence for treatment packages, but do not isolate the benefit of testing itself or establish improvement in social recovery. We propose a laboratory-clinical interpretation framework that links test selection and analytical verification to collaborative treatment review, while assessing psychological and social outcomes separately. Priorities include harmonized reporting, external validation of longitudinal decision rules, and pragmatic trials measuring retention, functioning, costs, and unintended consequences. Direct biomarkers are valuable measures of alcohol exposure; their contribution to rehabilitation depends on an appropriate clinical response to the result.

titre: Verbal learning and its impact on symptoms in adolescents with schizophrenia.
titre_fr: Verbal learning and its impact on symptoms in adolescents with schizophrenia.
auteurs: Ulloa Rosa Elena, Vega Daniela Giselle, Díaz Ricardo, Apiquian Rogelio, Mayer Pablo Adolfo
resume: Verbal learning develops substantially during adolescence and is consistently impaired in schizophrenia. Despite the severity of cognitive deficits in early-onset schizophrenia (EOS), verbal learning has not been systematically examined in adolescent patients. Understanding these impairments is essential due to their impact on academic, social, and functional outcomes. 106 adolescents (12-17 years) with schizophrenia or schizophreniform disorder (DSM-5) were recruited from inpatient and outpatient services in Mexico City. Assessments included the MINI-KID, Hopkins Verbal Learning Test-Revised (HVLT-R), and Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS). Descriptive analyzes, repeated-measures ANOVA, Cochran's Q test, and Pearson correlations were used to evaluate verbal learning performance and its associations with symptoms. Participants showed incremental learning across HVLT-R trials but low overall performance, recalling on average seven of 36 words. Intrusions and perseverations were infrequent yet related to poorer recall. Total correct words correlated negatively with negative symptoms, while semantic intrusions correlated positively with positive symptoms. Associations among HVLT-R variables indicated deficits in encoding, organization, and retrieval. Adolescents with schizophrenia exhibit significant verbal learning deficits linked to both negative, positive and general psychopathology symptoms. Early identification of these impairments is crucial for guiding targeted cognitive interventions. Larger, controlled studies are needed to refine these findings and support culturally relevant assessment and rehabilitation strategies.

Assessments included the MINI-KID, Hopkins Verbal Learning Test-Revised (HVLT-R), and Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS). Descriptive analyzes, repeated-measures ANOVA, Cochran's Q test, and Pearson correlations were used to evaluate verbal learning performance and its associations with symptoms. Participants showed incremental learning across HVLT-R trials but low overall performance, recalling on average seven of 36 words. Intrusions and perseverations were infrequent yet related to poorer recall. Total correct words correlated negatively with negative symptoms, while semantic intrusions correlated positively with positive symptoms. Associations among HVLT-R variables indicated deficits in encoding, organization, and retrieval. Adolescents with schizophrenia exhibit significant verbal learning deficits linked to both negative, positive and general psychopathology symptoms. Early identification of these impairments is crucial for guiding targeted cognitive interventions. Larger, controlled studies are needed to refine these findings and support culturally relevant assessment and rehabilitation strategies.

titre: Conductive Composite-Based Wearable Sensors for Sports Science: Intelligent Data Analysis and Emerging Applications.
titre_fr: Conductive Composite-Based Wearable Sensors for Sports Science: Intelligent Data Analysis and Emerging Applications.
auteurs: Wang Yutong, Ji Chaoxin, Shi Hongbo, Wang Wenda, Qi Qianrong, Li Yanjing, Liang Xiaoyue, Guan Qianhui, Zheng Minghao, Gao Xing, Cao Lianzhong
resume: Wearable sensors enable continuous acquisition of physiological, biochemical, and biomechanical signals during exercise, providing data to support sports performance assessment, training regulation, fatigue monitoring, and rehabilitation interventions. However, signal reliability and multidimensional data analysis under complex motion conditions remain constrained by device functionality. Conductive composites can improve sensor flexibility, interfacial conformability, and signal acquisition performance, while artificial intelligence (AI) enables movement pattern recognition, state assessment, and outcome prediction from complex data. Their integration is advancing wearable systems toward multimodal sensing and intelligent analysis. Guided by application needs in sports, this review summarizes emerging applications of wearable sensing technologies enabled by conductive composites and AI. First, the relevance to sports science and the data characteristics of physiological, biochemical, and biomechanical signals are introduced. The functional characteristics, representative applications, and major limitations of conductive polymer, carbon-based, MXene, and hydrogel composites are then summarized. Regarding algorithms, the fundamental principles of supervised learning, unsupervised learning, deep learning (DL), and large language models (LLMs) are discussed, with comparisons of their capabilities in feature extraction, temporal modeling, and multisource data analysis, as well as their input data requirements. On this basis, advances in the application of these systems to sports performance and sport-specific movement monitoring, exercise-induced fatigue monitoring and assessment, sports injury identification and evaluation, and intelligent monitoring of sports rehabilitation are reviewed followed by a discussion of current challenges and future directions. Through the coordinated integration of material design, signal acquisition, and intelligent analysis, wearable systems are expected to enable continuous, reliable, and individualized assessment of exercise-related states, with further applications in real-time feedback, risk alerts, and training decision support, providing a technological foundation for scientifically informed training, sports rehabilitation, and individual health management.

titre: Rethinking early arthrogenic muscle inhibition after total knee arthroplasty.
titre_fr: Rethinking early arthrogenic muscle inhibition after total knee arthroplasty.
auteurs: Qu Xia, Sun Guangxiang, Chen Bo
revue: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
resume: We read with interest the recent article by Barrera Uso et al. on early arthrogenic muscle inhibition (AMI) after total knee arthroplasty (TKA). The study provides clinically relevant evidence that AMI at 30 days strongly predicts persistence at 60 days. We suggest, however, that this finding should be interpreted as a prognostic association rather than evidence that 30-day AMI is the dominant biological determinant of subsequent inhibition. We also discuss the timing of postoperative assessment, noting that evaluation at 30 days is appropriate for studying persistence but less informative regarding the initial pathophysiological development of AMI. The Scientific Anterior Cruciate Ligament Network International (SANTI) classification has demonstrated excellent reliability in anterior cruciate ligament populations, although its generalizability to TKA remains to be specifically established. Finally, the absence of objective functional and patient-reported outcomes limits interpretation of the clinical significance of persistent AMI. Overall, the study identifies an important clinical phenotype and useful prognostic markers while leaving the underlying mechanisms of persistence to be further clarified.

titre: Naturalistic language assessment and brain-network biomarkers in post-stroke aphasia for precision neurorehabilitation.
titre_fr: Naturalistic language assessment and brain-network biomarkers in post-stroke aphasia for precision neurorehabilitation.
auteurs: Xia Jiayi, Pei Song, Zhou Song, Bai Yulong
resume: Advances in naturalistic language assessment, portable neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and brain-network modeling are creating new opportunities to evaluate post-stroke aphasia under conditions closer to real-world communication. Conventional aphasia batteries and isolated linguistic tasks remain essential for diagnosis, severity classification, and treatment planning, but they provide limited information about how language-network activity supports communication in dynamic, naturalistic contexts. This integrative review, informed by a structured literature search and descriptive thematic mapping, synthesizes evidence on connected speech, discourse production, narrative comprehension, interactive communication, and contextual reading after stroke. We examine how multilevel features from these behaviors can be organized into graded, interacting dimensions of lexical-semantic access, phonological encoding, grammatical organization, discourse processing, executive-predictive control, and speech-motor output. We further review multimodal evidence from fNIRS, fMRI, EEG/ERP, lesion-symptom mapping, structural connectivity, and functional connectivity, highlighting residual left-hemisphere language networks, conditional right-hemisphere support, bilateral reorganization, domain-general control systems, and longitudinal recovery. Portable EEG and fNIRS are considered complementary approaches for repeated assessment during less constrained language tasks, with distinct temporal, spatial, and practical trade-offs. Building on this evidence, we propose an operational ecological biomarker framework that links task choice, multilevel feature extraction, multivariate behavioral profiles, neural measures, prespecified clinical questions, and longitudinal outcomes. This framework may support recovery prediction, rehabilitation stratification, neuromodulation target selection, individualized therapy planning, and monitoring of functional communication.

titre: Motor action observation evaluation questionnaire: development and initial validity evidence for the scores in people with and without chronic low back pain.
titre_fr: Motor action observation evaluation questionnaire: development and initial validity evidence for the scores in people with and without chronic low back pain.
auteurs: La Touche Roy, Silván-Ferrero Prado, Nouvilas-Pallejá Encarnación, Paris-Alemany Alba, López-Rivero Alfonso J, Sorrel Miguel A
resume: Chronic low back pain (CLBP) is highly prevalent and associated with functional limitations. Although action observation is increasingly used as a cognitive-motor rehabilitation strategy, no brief instrument exists to assess how individuals appraise and understand movements during observation. The Questionnaire for the Assessment of Motor Action Observation (CENOAM) was developed using a sequential mixed-methods design. Phase 1 involved item generation based on literature review and qualitative analysis, followed by expert content validation using Aiken's V. Phase 2 consisted of a cross-sectional study including 280 participants (140 with CLBP and 140 asymptomatic). Dimensionality and psychometric properties of the CENOAM scores were examined using exploratory factor analysis, complementary dimensionality methods, internal consistency (α, ω), floor and ceiling effects, concurrent associations, and known-groups comparisons, following COSMIN recommendations. The final seven-item instrument showed a parsimonious two-dimensional structure, comprising Familiarity and Competence-Demand, supported by converging evidence across multiple methods. Internal consistency was high for both total and subscale scores, and no floor or ceiling effects were observed. CENOAM scores were positively associated with motor imagery ability, physical activity, and pain self-efficacy, and negatively associated with fear of movement. Participants with CLBP showed significantly lower scores than asymptomatic individuals across all dimensions, with large effect sizes. The CENOAM provides a brief and interpretable measure of movement appraisal during action observation. Its scores show initial evidence of validity and may support the individualization of action-observation-based rehabilitation in musculoskeletal conditions.

titre: Development and psychometric properties of the Prison Fellowship Good Citizenship Inventory (GCI): a values-based assessment for correctional settings.
titre_fr: Development and psychometric properties of the Prison Fellowship Good Citizenship Inventory (GCI): a values-based assessment for correctional settings.
auteurs: Denhof Michael, Scott Leigha, Hunsucker Chelsea, King Angela, Ferry Theresa
resume: This study aims to describe the development and psychometric validation of the Prison Fellowship Good Citizenship Inventory (GCI), a values-based assessment instrument designed to measure the internalization of six prosocial values (Community, Affirmation, Productivity, Restoration, Responsibility and Integrity) among prison program participants as an alternative to deficit-focused assessment approaches. Following multistage development, including item drafting, pilot testing and expert review, the GCI was administered to 559 prisoners across five state correctional facilities. Psychometric evaluation used principal axis factoring and confirmatory factor analysis to establish factor structure, with additional analyses examining internal consistency reliability, factorial invariance across gender, convergent validity (correlations with responsibility, conscientiousness and agreeableness measures) and criterion validity (associations with well-being, flourishing and criminogenic risk factors). Results supported a five-factor structure combining Responsibility and Integrity into a single dimension, with adequate internal consistency reliability (a = 0.66-0.86) across all scales. Factorial invariance testing confirmed measurement equivalence across gender groups. The GCI demonstrated significant convergent validity with established personality and responsibility measures (r = 0.42-0.57) and criterion validity through associations with human flourishing, psychological well-being and reduced antisocial characteristics, supporting the theorized relationships between prosocial values and positive outcomes. The GCI provides corrections professionals with a psychometrically sound, strengths-based assessment tool that evaluates program effectiveness beyond traditional recidivism metrics by measuring positive value development. This values-based approach offers a theoretically grounded alternative to risk-focused assessment models, aligning with emerging research on strength-based rehabilitation and desistance-focused interventions in correctional settings.

titre: Convergent validity of the Functional Bridge Test and its prognostic association with walking independence in patients with acute stroke: a retrospective cohort study.
titre_fr: Convergent validity of the Functional Bridge Test and its prognostic association with walking independence in patients with acute stroke: a retrospective cohort study.
auteurs: Sasa Naoki, Aoyagi Yoichiro, Wada Yuji
resume: The Functional Bridge Test (FBT) is a simple bedside assessment tool for evaluating hip elevation. It has demonstrated good validity and reliability in patients with lower limb hemiplegia after stroke and is significantly associated with stroke severity, lower limb strength, and basic mobility. However, its applicability across all patients with acute stroke, including those without lower limb hemiparesis, has not yet been established. This study aimed to examine the convergent validity of the FBT and its prognostic association with walking independence in patients with acute stroke. This study included consecutive patients with acute stroke admitted to a university hospital who survived and had complete data for outcome assessment. Convergent validity was evaluated using the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) total score, the NIHSS motor leg subscore on the affected side, and the Functional Status Score for the Intensive Care Unit (FSS-ICU), all measured on the first day of the rehabilitation program. The association between FBT grade and walking independence at a variable discharge-based endpoint, defined as the end of the inpatient rehabilitation program, was assessed through unadjusted and adjusted logistic regression analyses. Among 207 patients, the FBT grades were significantly correlated with the NIHSS total scores (ρ =  -0.668), the NIHSS motor leg subscores on the affected side (ρ =  -0.648), and the FSS-ICU scores (ρ = 0.730). The FBT was independently associated with walking independence (adjusted odds ratio = 1.786, 95% confidence interval = 1.022-3.418, p = .039). The FBT demonstrated adequate convergent validity and prognostic association in patients with acute stroke. This practical bedside assessment was associated with early functional status and walking independence at a variable discharge-based endpoint. Further prospective validation using standardized follow-up time points is needed.

titre: Development of an evidence-informed doctoral curriculum framework in physical therapy sciences: an international benchmarking and expert validation study.
titre_fr: Development of an evidence-informed doctoral curriculum framework in physical therapy sciences: an international benchmarking and expert validation study.
auteurs: Hazari Animesh, Kandakurti Praveen Kumar, Amaravadi Sampath Kumar, Agouris Ioannis, Jaiswal Varoon C, Venkatramana Manda
resume: The expanding scope of Physical Therapy research, coupled with rapid advances in digital health, artificial intelligence, implementation science, and evidence-based rehabilitation, has increased the demand for doctoral graduates with advanced research, leadership, and interdisciplinary competencies. Despite this evolution, published guidance describing systematic and evidence-informed approaches to developing doctoral curricula in Physical Therapy Sciences remains limited. This study aimed to develop and externally validate an evidence-informed doctoral curriculum framework through systematic needs assessment, international benchmarking, competency mapping, and constructive alignment. A multiphase evidence-informed curriculum development methodology was employed. The study comprised seven sequential phases: (1) needs assessment and environmental analysis; (2) international benchmarking; (3) comparative curriculum analysis; (4) competency mapping ; (5) Curriculum framework development; (6) Curriculum refinement and quality assurance; and (7) external expert content validation. Twenty-four doctoral programmes from research-intensive universities in the United Kingdom, United States, Canada, and Australia were screened, of which eighteen met the predefined inclusion criteria for benchmarking. The proposed curriculum was subsequently evaluated by an international panel of twelve experts using a structured validation instrument, and content validity was assessed using item-level and scale-level Content Validity Indices. Benchmarking demonstrated substantial consistency across international doctoral programmes in advanced research methodology, biostatistics, research ethics, scientific writing, proposal development, and independent dissertation research. Comparative analysis further identified increasing emphasis on digital health, artificial intelligence, implementation science, interdisciplinary collaboration, research leadership, and knowledge translation as emerging doctoral competencies. These findings informed the development of a competency-based doctoral curriculum aligned with internationally recognised educational frameworks. External expert validation demonstrated high perceived relevance, competency alignment, curriculum structure, content appropriateness, and implementation feasibility of the proposed framework, with domain-specific agreement ranging from 92% to 100%. Minor recommendations related to curriculum sequencing and emerging digital competencies were incorporated without altering the overall doctoral curriculum framework. This study presents an evidence-informed and high perceived relevance, alignment, and feasibility among an international expert panel that aligns Physical Therapy Sciences education with contemporary international educational standards and evolving rehabilitation research priorities. The proposed framework offers a transparent methodology for curriculum development that integrates systematic benchmarking, competency mapping, and expert validation, providing a practical model to inform the development or revision of doctoral programmes in Physical Therapy and related health professions. Future implementation studies are warranted to evaluate its educational effectiveness across diverse institutional settings.

titre: Robotic Assessment of Thumb Proprioception after Stroke: Reliability, Validity, and Sensitivity.
titre_fr: Robotic Assessment of Thumb Proprioception after Stroke: Reliability, Validity, and Sensitivity.
auteurs: Garcia-Fernandez Luis, Farrens Andria J, Chan Vicky, Rojas Raymond D, Wolbrecht Eric T, Perry Joel C, Do An H, Cramer Steven C, Reinkensmeyer David J
revue: Archives of physical medicine and rehabilitation
resume: Despite the thumb's critical role in dexterity and its dense sensory innervation, thumb proprioceptive deficits after stroke remain limited due to the limited nature of clinical assessments. This study evaluated the reliability, validity, and sensitivity of a novel robotic assessment of thumb proprioception, SomatoCircleJump (SCJ), in individuals with chronic stroke. Cross-sectional psychometric study evaluating the reliability, validity and sensitivity of SCJ using baseline data from a clinical trial, with assessments conducted twice 5-10 days apart. In SCJ, a robot moved the visually occluded thumb, and participants indicated when the thumb passed a visual target. University-based rehabilitation research laboratory. Thirty-five stroke survivors with residual unilateral hand weakness and 24 healthy age-matched controls. Not applicable. SCJ proprioceptive error, defined as the angular difference between actual thumb position and the visually presented target. Test-retest reliability was assessed with Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC). Validity and sensitivity were evaluated by comparing SCJ with the Fugl-Meyer Assessment Sensory Scale for the upper extremity (FMA-S) thumb position item, and two robotic proprioception tests, one for the thumb (ThumbSense) and one for the fingers (Crisscross). SCJ demonstrated good test-retest reliability (ICC = 0.82, 95% CI [0.72-0.87]). SCJ error correlated significantly with FMA-S (ρ = -0.56, p < 0.001), ThumbSense accuracy (ρ = -0.62, p < 0.001), and Crisscross error (ρ = 0.61, p < 0.001). Using a 2SD criterion relative to controls, SCJ identified thumb proprioceptive impairment in 61% of stroke participants, compared with 23% identified by FMA-S. SCJ is a reliable, valid, and sensitive assessment of dynamic thumb proprioception after stroke. It revealed that thumb proprioceptive deficits are common and related to finger proprioception deficits, supporting its use in future studies of sensory impairment and rehabilitation outcomes.

titre: Design and analysis of an affordable manual sit-to-stand wheelchair for disabled individuals.
titre_fr: Design and analysis of an affordable manual sit-to-stand wheelchair for disabled individuals.
auteurs: Tiwari Tushar, Dan Pranab K
resume: The individuals with lower-limb disabilities often experience considerable difficulty during sit-to-stand (STS) transitions, limiting their independence and increasing reliance on caregivers. According to the World Health Organisation (WHO, 2023), nearly 80 million people worldwide require wheelchairs. This study presents the design and performance evaluation of an affordable manual sit-to-stand wheelchair that incorporates ergonomic and anthropometric design principles with a three-bar linkage mechanism, ball screw drive, scissor-lift structure, force-balancing mechanism, and optimised gear ratio to ensure stable, controlled, and energy-efficient operation without electrical actuators. Structural validation of design using finite element analysis demonstrated a maximum frame deformation of 2.2 mm and a factor of safety of 2.5 under a static load of 120 kg, confirming the mechanical reliability of the design. Human testing is conducted with 25 participants (15 wheelchair users and 10 healthy volunteers), while clinical evaluation is performed under a physiotherapist's supervision using standardised functional assessment protocols. The average sit-to-stand transition time is 9.5 ± 1.8 s, with 90% of participants achieving successful independent standing. Force analysis indicated that the proposed linkage mechanism reduced the operating force to approximately 10 N, corresponding to a 45.6% reduction in user effort. Furthermore, usability assessment yielded a mean System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 86.3/100, indicating excellent user acceptance. The findings demonstrate that the proposed STS wheelchair is a safe, mechanically robust, and cost-effective assistive mobility solution that enhances user independence, reduces caregiver burden, and improves the quality of life for individuals with mobility impairments, particularly in low-resource settings.
