titre: Functional Strength in Children with Developmental Disabilities: An Exploratory Comparison of Three Clinical Cohorts Including Children with Developmental Coordination Disorder, Intellectual Disabilities, and Cerebral Palsy.
titre_fr: Functional Strength in Children with Developmental Disabilities: An Exploratory Comparison of Three Clinical Cohorts Including Children with Developmental Coordination Disorder, Intellectual Disabilities, and Cerebral Palsy.
auteurs: Aertssen Wendy, Steenbergen Bert, Smits-Engelsman Bouwien
resume: Background: This study presents an exploratory comparison of data from three previously collected clinical cohorts. The first aim was to compare functional strength performance among a cohort of children with Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD), Intellectual Disabilities (ID), and Cerebral Palsy (CP). The second aim was to examine whether the associations between age and functional strength performance differed across these cohorts. Methods: Data from 103 children aged 7-10 years (29 DCD, 47 ID, 27 CP) were combined. Functional Strength Measurement (FSM, FSM-ID, FSM-CP) scores were compared with reference norms. Cohort differences were examined using multivariate analysis of covariance (MANCOVA) with body weight included as a covariate. Associations between age and FSM performance were examined using General Linear Models including age, clinical cohort, and age-by-cohort interaction terms. Results: Compared with the FSM reference norms, 17-89% of participants were classified as impaired or at risk for muscle-power performance, while 62-92% demonstrated limitations in muscle-endurance tasks. Significant differences between the three clinical cohorts were observed for overarm throwing, underarm throwing, lifting a box, and stair climbing, with medium effect sizes. Evidence for age-by-cohort interactions was observed for overarm throwing, underarm throwing, standing long jump, and sit-to-stand performance, indicating that associations between age and functional-strength performance differed across clinical cohorts. Conclusions: Children in the clinical cohorts demonstrated lower levels of functional-strength performance than typically developing peers. Functional-strength profiles differed across clinical cohorts. However, as the data were derived from three distinct cohorts rather than collected within a single study, and minor differences exist between the FSM, FSM-ID and FSM-CP, the findings should be interpreted with caution and considered hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. Furthermore, because the data were cross-sectional, no conclusions can be drawn regarding developmental changes over time. These findings may help generate hypotheses for future assessment, intervention and longitudinal research in children with developmental disabilities.

titre: Modulation of Simulated Microgravity-Induced Behavioral Responses by Caffeine in Zebrafish: A Pilot Study.
titre_fr: Modulation of Simulated Microgravity-Induced Behavioral Responses by Caffeine in Zebrafish: A Pilot Study.
auteurs: Ionescu Cǎtǎlina, Di Domenicantonio Irene, Cardone Franco, Sbriccoli Marco, Pînzariu Alin Constantin, Novac Bogdan, Novac Otilia, Hogas Mihai, Ciobîcă Alin
resume: This pilot study evaluates the effects of acute caffeine administration on adult zebrafish behavioral responses under simulated microgravity, aiming to understand how common dietary stimulants modulate neurobehavioral adaptations in altered-gravity environments. Adult zebrafish were immersed in 25 mg/L caffeine for 30 min, followed by a 1 h exposure to simulated microgravity using a clinostat system, before immediate assessment in a standard locomotor test and a vertical Novel Tank Test tracked via EthoVision XT 14 software. While independent exposures to caffeine or microgravity yielded minimal modifications to baseline swimming kinetics, their simultaneous application resulted in an increased hyperlocomotor response, characterized by increased distance moved, average velocity, and moving duration. Co-exposure also altered stereotypic motor coordination, significantly enhancing clockwise rotations. Furthermore, dual-view heat maps in the Novel Tank Test showed that the simultaneous exposure to caffeine and microgravity showed altered wall-associated spatial behavior (thigmotaxis) and bottom-dwelling avoidance, shifting behavioral output toward active vertical exploration and central arena habituation. These results suggest that simulated microgravity may influence the psychopharmacological expression of caffeine, with the combined exposure being associated with altered vertical exploration and motor activity, thereby supporting the potential utility of adult zebrafish as an experimental model for space biomedical research and highlighting the complex role of dietary countermeasures in altered-gravity environments.

titre: A fuzzy-augmented deep learning pipeline for multilingual natural language processing from handwritten script: a Tamil case study.
titre_fr: A fuzzy-augmented deep learning pipeline for multilingual natural language processing from handwritten script: a Tamil case study.
auteurs: Kumar A Harsha, Aarthi B, Kumaran K, Saranya G, Venkatram C Preetham
resume: Multilingual natural language processing (NLP) from handwritten script is an open artificial intelligence (AI) challenge requiring advances in both pattern recognition and sequence generation. Existing end-to-end pipelines often fail to model the structural uncertainty in complex scripts, particularly the decorative stroke variability in Dravidian writing systems, before passing representations to downstream NLP models. This omission can result in error propagation from the recognition stage into translation. This paper proposes a Tamil Handwritten Character Recognition and Translation (THCRT) framework, a fuzzy-augmented deep learning NLP pipeline that addresses this gap by coupling a Biparametric Exponential Membership Function-based Fuzzy Inference System (BEMFFIS) with a deep convolutional recognition network and a multilingual transformer for translation. The fuzzy inference component models stroke-boundary uncertainty through Decorative Stroke Analysis (DSA) using the Coefficient of Variation (CoV). BEMFFIS employs a coupled-parameter Gaussian membership function, which reduces the hyperparameter search space to a single degree of freedom. This produces normalized representations that improve downstream NLP performance. Hierarchical segmentation of line, word, and character is achieved via Connected Polar Functional Component Analysis (CPFCA). Recognition is performed by a Global Averaged Excitation-based Deep Convolutional Neural Network with Swish activation (GAE-DCSSNN), and multilingual translation is executed by a multilingual Bernoulli Distribution-based Auto-Regressive Transformer (mBBDART) built on the mBART backbone with stochastic token-pruning augmentation. The pipeline is evaluated on Tamil handwriting using two publicly available datasets: the Tamil Offline Handwritten Word Recognition (TOHWR) dataset and the Tamil Handwritten Character Corpus Mendeley Data (THCCMD) dataset. Translation quality is assessed on a 1,200-sample parallel reference set annotated by two certified bilingual translators with Cohen's κ = 0.91, reflecting the word-level and short-phrase scope of the TOHWR corpus. The THCRT framework achieves a recognition accuracy of 98.23%, a Character Error Rate (CER) of 1.12%, and a Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU) score of 0.438 on the annotated evaluation set, outperforming the baseline architectures on both datasets and demonstrating a 1.79 percentage-point accuracy gain attributed to the BEMFFIS stroke-uncertainty module.

titre: Contact-Free Human-Machine Interfaces via Printed Thermopile Infrared Arrays.
titre_fr: Contact-Free Human-Machine Interfaces via Printed Thermopile Infrared Arrays.
auteurs: Wang Zirui, Luo Nan, Bose Amrutha, Khan Muhammad Irfan, Liu Jiayi, Klinder Leon Viktor, Franke Leonard, Hussein Mohamed, Lemmer Uli, Mallick Md Mofasser
resume: Human-machine interfaces (HMIs) are evolving as key components for advanced sensing in communication and control systems. In particular, contact-free HMIs can facilitate unique advantages in hygiene, durability, and non-destructive sensing. However, spatially resolved sensing platforms remain challenging using bulk approaches. Here, we report flexible infrared interface arrays (TIA1 and TIA2) with ≥10 pixels that exploit the photo-thermoelectric (PTE) infrared sensing properties of Bi-Te-based thermoelectric (TE) materials via a dual-stage energy conversion process: radiation-to-thermal, followed by thermal-to-electric. The p- and n-type TE materials and electrodes were printed on polyimide to fabricate TIAs. After encapsulation with a black absorber, radially patterned silver mirrors are printed on the outer part of the pixels using aerosol jet-printing to partially shield each thermocouple. This induces a localized temperature gradient, hence an output voltage via the Seebeck effect under infrared illumination. The pixels exhibit responsivities of 0.7 VW<sup>-1</sup> (TIA1) and 0.9 VW<sup>-1</sup> (TIA2), respectively, under CO<sub>2</sub> laser irradiation (10.6 µm), with pixel-to-pixel variation within ± 10%. The TIAs were demonstrated as non-contact handwriting and dialing interfaces, converting human gestures into digital signals. These results pave the way for a self-powered and contactless interface for future human-machine interaction technologies.

titre: Effects of Spatial Constraint on Bare-Hand Logographic Character Handwriting Performance in Virtual Reality.
titre_fr: Effects of Spatial Constraint on Bare-Hand Logographic Character Handwriting Performance in Virtual Reality.
auteurs: Cheng Xinru, Zhang Yining, Wei Yushi, Jiang Rui, Hansen Preben, Liang Hai-Ning
revue: IEEE transactions on visualization and computer graphics
resume: Spatial constraints significantly influence motor performance in virtual reality (VR), as interactions often involve hands hovering in mid-air. Yet their specific impact on logographic handwriting, such as Chinese and similar characters, remains underexplored. While VR text entry research is predominantly alphabetic-centric, especially English, handwriting support for complex scripts is fragmented across systems that treat physical or virtual guidance as implementation details rather than analytical or design variables. To address this, we compare three spatial constraint forms under a unified input pipeline: Unconstrained Mid-Air, Virtual Collision Surfaces, and Anchored Physical Surfaces. In a 3×3 within-subjects study (N = 24) with users writing Chinese characters of various complexity, we identified a critical stability-efficiency trade-off. While constrained conditions (virtual and physical) reduced trajectory length and rewrite counts, they increased normalized writing and total input time compared to mid-air input. Subjectively, U-MAH was rated as the most usable. Compared with HVS, HAVS reduced physical and temporal demand while still producing shorter trajectories and fewer rewrites than U-MAH. We also contribute design implications on when freer mid-air input may be preferable and when planar or physically supported writing may be more beneficial in VR handwriting.
resume_fr: Spatial constraints significantly influence motor performance in virtual reality (VR), as interactions often involve hands hovering in mid-air. Yet their specific impact on logographic handwriting, such as Chinese and similar characters, remains underexplored. While VR text entry research is predominantly alphabetic-centric, especially English, handwriting support for complex scripts is fragmented across systems that treat physical or virtual guidance as implementation details rather than analytical or design variables. To address this, we compare three spatial constraint forms under a unified input pipeline: Unconstrained Mid-Air, Virtual Collision Surfaces, and Anchored Physical Surfaces. In a 3×3 within-subjects study (N = 24) with users writing Chinese characters of various complexity, we identified a critical stability-efficiency trade-off. While constrained conditions (virtual and physical) reduced trajectory length and rewrite counts, they increased normalized writing and total input time compared to mid-air input. Subjectively, U-MAH was rated as the most usable. Compared with HVS, HAVS reduced physical and temporal demand while still producing shorter trajectories and fewer rewrites than U-MAH. We also contribute design implications on when freer mid-air input may be preferable and when planar or physically supported writing may be more beneficial in VR handwriting.

titre: The word superiority effect: modulation by language familiarity, handwriting, and inversion.
titre_fr: The word superiority effect: modulation by language familiarity, handwriting, and inversion.
auteurs: Singh Mehar, Feizabadi Monireh, Albonico Andrea, Barton Jason J S
resume: Literate humans are expert in reading text. On proposed reflection of this expertise is a whole-word influence on the identification of letters. In the present study, we investigate the word superiority effect, and how language familiarity, orientation and script regularity modulate this effect. We recruited two groups of 20 subjects, one fluent in Farsi and one in Punjabi. Members of neither group were familiar with the other group's language. We presented four-letter words or pseudowords briefly, following which subjects had to indicate which of two letters had been part of the four-letter stimulus. We present blocks with Farsi and Punjabi separately, as well as upright or inverted stimuli separately, to measure the impact of both language familiarity as well as experience with orientation, given that most of a subject's exposure to text is with upright words. Within blocks we varied whether stimuli were shown in a computer font or in handwriting. We found a significant word superiority effect for the familiar language but none for the unfamiliar language. For the familiar language, the word superiority effect was greater for upright stimuli, but still present with inverted stimuli. The word superiority effect was of similar magnitude for font and handwritten text. We conclude that the whole-word influences that generate the word superiority effect arise solely through experience with a language and depend strongly on the learned orientation of text, but are not modulated by script regularity.

titre: A Preliminary Study of the Immediate Effects of Spherical-Grip and Palmar-Support Handwriting Assistive Devices on Handwriting Kinematics During Numeric Copying in Children with Disabilities.
titre_fr: A Preliminary Study of the Immediate Effects of Spherical-Grip and Palmar-Support Handwriting Assistive Devices on Handwriting Kinematics During Numeric Copying in Children with Disabilities.
auteurs: Yun Seong Ho, Eun Seon-Deok
resume: Background: Children with disabilities may experience difficulty with handwriting due to motor impairments that limit their ability to grasp and manipulate a pen. Objectives: This preliminary exploratory study investigated the effects of handwriting assistive devices (ADs) on handwriting kinematics in children with disabilities. Methods: A quasi-experimental within-subject repeated-measures design was used. Seven children with disabilities affecting hand function participated in this study. The children performed a numeric copying task under three conditions: no assistive device (no-AD), spherical-grip AD, and palmar-support AD. Handwriting kinematics were measured and compared across the three conditions. Results: The spherical-grip AD was associated with shorter writing duration and path length than the no-AD condition. No other statistically significant differences were observed among the three conditions. Applications: Our findings should be interpreted as AD-related differences in handwriting kinematics rather than as evidence of improved handwriting performance because handwriting quality was not assessed and path length was not normalized for numeral size. Nevertheless, quantitative kinematic assessment may provide objective information for evaluating handwriting ADs and for understanding how different device designs influence handwriting movement characteristics in children with disabilities.

titre: Pen-Based Graphomotor Measures for Early Identification of Attention-Related Difficulties in Preschool Children: A Conceptual and Critical Narrative Review.
titre_fr: Pen-Based Graphomotor Measures for Early Identification of Attention-Related Difficulties in Preschool Children: A Conceptual and Critical Narrative Review.
auteurs: Ji Muxian, Du Tingshu, Ma Tingting, Hu Luming
resume: Attention problems may compromise child development, learning, behavioral regulation, and school adjustment. The preschool years are an important period for early identification because attentional control develops rapidly and supports the transition to formal schooling. Existing assessment approaches, however, provide limited information about how attentional regulation unfolds during ongoing behavior. This non-systematic narrative review synthesizes evidence from preschool attention assessment, graphomotor development, digital handwriting, and measurement theory using a targeted, concept-driven approach. No systematic literature search or formal study-selection protocol was employed. It proposes pen-based graphomotor attention measurement (PGAM) as a measurement-development framework for examining how children select relevant information, maintain task goals, monitor movement, and correct deviations during graphomotor activity. PGAM links theoretically specified attentional demands and continuous pen-trajectory data to dynamic patterns of engagement, maintenance, disruption, and recovery during goal-directed behavior. Available evidence supports the technical feasibility of digital graphomotor recording and suggests associations between attention-related functioning and graphomotor organization. Future studies should first establish the reliability and developmental calibration of PGAM. Subsequent work should evaluate construct and incremental validity and decision utility to determine whether these process measures can support attention-specific interpretation and potential screening use.

titre: Handwriting-based Alzheimer's disease classification on the DARWIN dataset: Repeated nested validation, task-level reduction, and cross-validated explainability.
titre_fr: Handwriting-based Alzheimer's disease classification on the DARWIN dataset: Repeated nested validation, task-level reduction, and cross-validated explainability.
auteurs: Fatima Tehreem, Lashari Tahira Anwar, Moetesum Momina, Lashari Sana Anwar
resume: Online handwriting provides a low-burden source of cognitive-motor measurements, but small datasets can yield optimistic results when preprocessing, task selection, or explanation is not separated from evaluation. We evaluated eight classifiers on the DARWIN dataset (174 participants; 25 tasks; 450 predictors) using ten repetitions of 5-outer/3-inner-fold nested stratified cross-validation. All preprocessing, hyperparameter selection, and calibration were restricted to outer training data. We added a training-derived operating point, fully nested seven-task selection, cross-model subset transfer, foldwise SHAP analysis, and an all-feature SHAP sensitivity analysis. Random Forest had the highest descriptive ROC-AUC (0.938 ± 0.033 across 50 held-out folds). The Friedman omnibus test indicated model differences (p < 0.001), but no one of 28 paired comparisons remained significant after Holm correction. Training-derived thresholds (median 0.461) yielded held-out sensitivity 0.869 and specificity 0.831; these are exploratory operating characteristics, not a clinical cutoff. Nested seven-task selection achieved AUC 0.916 ± 0.037, compared with 0.956 ± 0.030 for all 25 tasks, and selected subsets were unstable (mean Jaccard 0.195). Cross-validated SHAP emphasized temporal variables, although an all-450-feature sensitivity analysis showed that individual ranks depend partly on ANOVA preselection. The study contributes an integrated, leakage-controlled evaluation rather than a new classifier or a validated diagnostic instrument; external prospective validation remains necessary.

titre: The impact of cognitive processes associated with image recognition on visuo-vestibular interaction.
titre_fr: The impact of cognitive processes associated with image recognition on visuo-vestibular interaction.
auteurs: Malara Pasquale, Tosin Andrea Giorgia, Castellucci Andrea, Martellucci Salvatore, Musumano Lucia Belén, Mandalà Marco
revue: Journal of vestibular research : equilibrium & orientation
resume: An increasing number of articles in the literature highlight the importance of saccadic remodulation in compensatory mechanisms, and the reappearance of SHIMP saccades following a vestibular insult correlates strongly with an improvement in symptoms reported by patients on the DHI. To assess the influence of attentional processes and working memory on visuo-vestibular interaction, we designed three independent yet interrelated experiments.In the first two experiments, perfectly healthy subjects (first experiment) and patients with a history of unilateral or bilateral vestibular deficits (second experiment) underwent vHIT in SHIMP mode and the Functional Head Impulse Test. The two tests were performed in the same session, initially separately ("separate protocol") and subsequently simultaneously ("combined protocol"). The mean latency of SHIMP saccades and their degree of clustering were analyzed, and finally, the recognition rate of the Landolt C. Subsequently, any variations in these parameters between the "disjoint protocol" and the "joint protocol" were assessed, and, in the second experiment, the differences between the "disjoint protocol" and the "joint protocol" were correlated with the severity of symptoms measured by the DHI. The aim was to verify whether, during the "joint protocol," the near-simultaneity of the two tasks, both mediated by shared parietal cortical substrates, altered any parameters. In the third experiment, we used vHIT in HIMP mode and fHIT, performed in disjointed and joint protocols. The objective was to verify whether the conjunction of saccadic function and cognitive load related to recognition could influence the latency and clustering of recovery saccades favorably.Conclusions: Results suggest visual recognition impacts visuo-vestibular interaction, supporting integrated dual-task protocols for ecological balance assessment and resolving clinical discrepancies, though larger multicenter studies are needed to confirm these preliminary findings.

titre: Beyond the skull: Neuropsychological rehabilitation and Extended/Distributed Cognition.
titre_fr: Beyond the skull: Neuropsychological rehabilitation and Extended/Distributed Cognition.
auteurs: Salas Christian, Rossi Alejandra, Rojas-Líbano Daniel, Kausel Leonie, Parada Francisco J
resume: BackgroundNeuropsychological Rehabilitation has traditionally relied on models that conceptualize cognition primarily as a property of the individual brain. However, many established rehabilitation practices extend beyond the individual, involving cognitive artifacts (e.g., tools), modifications of the physical environment, and the coordinated contribution of other people. This creates a potential mismatch between how cognition is theoretically conceptualized and how rehabilitation is practiced.ObjectiveIn this conceptual article, we examine how Extended and Distributed Cognition may help address this discrepancy. Drawing on the historical work of Kurt Goldstein, contemporary cognitive science, and evidence-based rehabilitation practice, we distinguish Extended Cognition, which emphasizes how external resources can become integrated into an individual's cognitive processes, from Distributed Cognition, which examines how cognitive activity is organized across people, artifacts, and environments.ImplicationsWe argue that these perspectives broaden both the unit of analysis and the potential targets of rehabilitation: intervention may involve not only changing cognitive processes within the individual, but also introducing or reorganizing cognitive artifacts, modifying environments, and changing how other people interact with the person. Established practices including external compensatory strategies, communication partner training, environmental modification, and the coordinated organization of rehabilitation teams illustrate the clinical relevance of this perspective.ConclusionExtended and Distributed Cognition may therefore provide a complementary theoretical framework for understanding how cognition is supported and reorganized in everyday life after brain injury, helping to bridge the persistent gap between neuropsychological mechanisms and everyday functioning.

titre: Comparison of Postural Control During Activities of Daily Living Between Trained Individuals With Parkinson's Disease and Healthy Older Adults With Different Exercise Levels.
titre_fr: Comparison of Postural Control During Activities of Daily Living Between Trained Individuals With Parkinson's Disease and Healthy Older Adults With Different Exercise Levels.
auteurs: Pereira Larissa Alessandra, Gonçalves Broto Patrícia, Araújo Hayslenne Andressa Gonçalves Oliveira, Miri Andressa Leticia, Barboza Natália Mariano, Terra Marcelle Brandão, Smaili Suhaila Mahmoud
revue: Journal of aging and physical activity
resume: The aim of this study was to compare postural control (PC) during activities of daily living between trained individuals with Parkinson's disease and healthy individuals who practiced physical exercise and those who did not. This is a case-control study, in which 105 individuals were assigned to groups: 35 individuals with Parkinson's disease who underwent neurofunctional physiotherapy (GDP-T), 35 healthy individuals who practiced exercise (G-EX), and 35 healthy individuals who did not practice exercise (G-NEX). The Activities-specific Balance Confidence Scale was used to assess participants. PC was assessed by posturography in the following conditions: (a) bipedal position, (b) feeding task, (c) getting dressed task, and (d) executive function task. The parameters evaluated were center of pressure (COP) area (in square centimeters), amplitude (in centimeters), and anteroposterior and mediolateral speed (in centimeters per second). GDP-T showed less balance confidence than the other groups. There was no significant difference between the groups in the bipedal position. G-NEX showed a greater COP area, amplitude, and speed of movement (anteroposterior and mediolateral) compared with G-EX and GDP-T in the functional tasks. G-EX showed a smaller COP area in the getting dressed task and greater speed in executive function compared with GDP-T. The PC of GDP-T was similar to that of G-EX, although its balance confidence was lower. G-NEX showed greater variation in the COP parameters for the variables analyzed in all tasks. Significance/Implications: Regular exercise has been shown to overcome the clinical characteristics of Parkinson's disease and provide a positive PC response to specialized training in both typical and atypical aging.

titre: Childhood trauma and dimensions of criminal thinking in individuals referred for forensic psychiatric evaluation.
titre_fr: Childhood trauma and dimensions of criminal thinking in individuals referred for forensic psychiatric evaluation.
auteurs: Şahin Hüseyin Çağrı, Koyuncu Oğuzhan, Altunç Ali Tarık, Çiçek Ümit, Merzifonlu Zeynep, Namlı Ahmet Naim, Kırbıyık Faruk, Demirel Muhammed, Boylu Muhammed Emin, Turan Şenol
resume: Childhood trauma has been consistently associated with criminal behavior, yet its relationship with criminal thinking remains understudied. This single-center, cross-sectional study examined the associations between childhood trauma and dimensions of criminal thinking among individuals referred for criminal responsibility evaluation. Eighty-four individuals evaluated at the Observation Department of the Council of Forensic Medicine, a national referral center in Türkiye, completed the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire-Short Form and the Criminal Thinking Scale. Associations between the total and subscale scores were examined using correlation analysis followed by simple linear regression analysis. Mean age of the participants was 36.98 ± 10.79 years. CTS total score was not significantly associated with the CTQ-SF total or subscale scores. Power Orientation was the only criminal-thinking dimension significantly associated with the total childhood trauma score (ρ = 0.318, p = 0.003). Power Orientation was also positively correlated with emotional abuse (ρ = 0.334, p = 0.002) and sexual abuse (ρ = 0.290, p = 0.007). In the unadjusted regression model, higher total childhood trauma scores were associated with higher Power Orientation scores (β = 0.338, p = 0.002), accounting for 11.4% of the variance (R<sup>2</sup> = 0.114); the association remained significant after adjustment for age, education, substance use, prior incarceration, and offense group (β = 0.326, p = 0.002, model R<sup>2</sup> = 0.254). These findings indicate that childhood trauma may be associated with specific dimensions of criminal thinking rather than generalized criminal cognition. Associations of emotional and sexual abuse with power-oriented thinking suggest that different forms of childhood trauma may be linked to distinct offense-related cognitive styles and support the potential value of trauma-informed approaches in forensic psychiatric assessment and rehabilitation.

titre: White matter microstructural biomarkers predict cochlear implant outcomes in adults with postlingual deafness.
titre_fr: White matter microstructural biomarkers predict cochlear implant outcomes in adults with postlingual deafness.
auteurs: Grégoire Anaïs M, Delinte Nicolas, Dricot Laurence, Deggouj Naïma, Kupers Ron
resume: Although cochlear implantation (CI) has been used for decades to restore hearing in sensorineural deafness, accurately predicting individual outcomes remains challenging-particularly in adults with postlingual deafness, a population that has been relatively understudied. In our previous work, we showed that speech comprehension after 6 months of CI use is better predicted when preoperative grey matter volume and cortical thickness in regions supporting language and cognition are considered alongside preoperative residual hearing and audiovisual abilities. In the present study, we investigated whether preoperative diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) metrics in subcortical white matter (WM) could account for individual variability in cochlear implant adaptation and enhance predictive accuracy. Thereto, we collected preoperative DWI and speech performance under auditory-only and audiovisual conditions in 65 adults with postlingual bilateral deafness. Improvement in speech comprehension with CI was evaluated at 6 and 12 months post-implantation. A whole-brain analysis revealed significant positive correlations between preoperative fractional anisotropy (FA) within a cluster in the left arcuate fasciculus and speech perception at 6 months in both auditory-only and audiovisual conditions. Incorporating FA from the arcuate fasciculus cluster into the multiple linear regression model developed in our previous study significantly improved prediction accuracy for CI outcomes at 6 months. We also identified FA clusters in the right inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus and the corpus callosum that showed positive relationships with audiovisual comprehension and mid-term cochlear implant performance. In contrast, mean FA values averaged across entire tracts did not show similarly strong associations with speech perception, as shown after tract reconstruction. Notably, sex modulated the relationship between age and FA values across multiple white matter clusters. These findings underscore the role of localized WM microstructural properties in shaping speech adaptation after CI. Identifying WM-based predictors of CI performance may aid clinicians in forecasting individual outcomes and tailoring rehabilitation strategies, particularly for patients at risk of delayed or limited benefit. Further research is needed to clarify the origins of regional FA variability.

titre: How the Design of Technology-Mediated Cognitive Training Paradigms Impacts Efficacy in Childhood Cancer Survivors: A Systematic Review.
titre_fr: How the Design of Technology-Mediated Cognitive Training Paradigms Impacts Efficacy in Childhood Cancer Survivors: A Systematic Review.
auteurs: O'Loughlin Rebekah J, Semendric Ines, Pope Kenneth J, Hobbs David A, Collins-Praino Lyndsey E
resume: Background/Objectives: Cancer and its subsequent treatments have been shown to cause significant cognitive impairment, known as Cancer-Related Cognitive Impairment (CRCI). CRCI impacts a range of cognitive domains, including working memory and executive function, attention, concentration, short-term memory, visuospatial control, problem solving, and information processing speed. Treatment options for these cancer sequelae are limited, with many patients never receiving any medical rehabilitation efforts. Current treatment recommendations include pharmaceutical intervention, cognitive training (CT), physical activity, and self-management strategies, with a prior meta-analysis in adults supporting CT as the most promising of these options. Thus, this systematic review aims to explore the current body of evidence for the use of CT as a treatment for childhood cancer survivors and assess the strengths and weaknesses of previously utilised programs to determine how to best test and optimise CT for this population. Methods: A systematic search was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, PsycINFO and CINAHL. The review was prepared following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 reporting guidelines. Results: From an initial 6172 studies, six were included in the final review, covering 208 intervention participants who completed CT. CT platforms used by the included studies were all technology-mediated, and consisted of 'Cogmed' (n = 4), Attention Process Training (n = 1) and 'Captain's log' (n = 1). Cognitive testing in the included studies covered three domains: working memory, attention and delayed recall (memory). Studies showed varied improvement across these domains, with most positive effects in the domain of working memory, although certainty of evidence across the included studies was all assessed as low or very low. resume_fr: Background/Objectives: Cancer and its subsequent treatments have been shown to cause significant cognitive impairment, known as Cancer-Related Cognitive Impairment (CRCI). CRCI impacts a range of cognitive domains, including working memory and executive function, attention, concentration, short-term memory, visuospatial control, problem solving, and information processing speed. Treatment options for these cancer sequelae are limited, with many patients never receiving any medical rehabilitation efforts. Current treatment recommendations include pharmaceutical intervention, cognitive training (CT), physical activity, and self-management strategies, with a prior meta-analysis in adults supporting CT as the most promising of these options. Thus, this systematic review aims to explore the current body of evidence for the use of CT as a treatment for childhood cancer survivors and assess the strengths and weaknesses of previously utilised programs to determine how to best test and optimise CT for this population. Methods: A systematic search was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, PsycINFO and CINAHL. The review was prepared following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 reporting guidelines. Results: From an initial 6172 studies, six were included in the final review, covering 208 intervention participants who completed CT. CT platforms used by the included studies were all technology-mediated, and consisted of 'Cogmed' (n = 4), Attention Process Training (n = 1) and 'Captain's log' (n = 1). Cognitive testing in the included studies covered three domains: working memory, attention and delayed recall (memory). Studies showed varied improvement across these domains, with most positive effects in the domain of working memory, although certainty of evidence across the included studies was all assessed as low or very low. Conclusions: This systematic review provides preliminary evidence for the use of CT in childhood cancer survivors, but also makes a range of recommendations for future studies in this population, given the current gaps in the literature. This includes utilisation of a control group, use of consistent cognitive testing protocols, and CT design that targets the diverse nature of the cognitive change seen in CRCI. Together, these recommendations will allow future studies to more fully probe the utility of CT as an intervention for this population, while also optimising its usage.

titre: Brain-Computer Interfaces for Cognitive Rehabilitation: A Narrative Review.
titre_fr: Brain-Computer Interfaces for Cognitive Rehabilitation: A Narrative Review.
auteurs: Cantillo-Negrete Jessica, Rodríguez-García Martín Emiliano, Carrillo-Mora Paul, Méndez-Gómez Dalia Danely, Carino-Escobar Ruben I
resume: Cognitive diseases/disorders are a major cause of disability affecting millions of people worldwide due to pathologies or conditions such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, vascular cognitive impairment, and attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder. The effects of these diseases/disorders can range from subjective cognitive complaints to mild cognitive impairment and even dementia that can affect multiple cognitive domains, causing disability and alterations in daily functioning and quality of life. Cognitive training has been researched as a potential therapeutic option for treating cognitive disability. In particular, cognitive training delivered using brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) represents a promising technology for cognitive rehabilitation. For this reason, this work presents a narrative review aimed at bridging the clinical aspects of cognition performance and the technical features of BCI systems. Additionally, it reports on the current advances of BCIs for cognitive rehabilitation in the pathologies/conditions that are the main contributors of cognitive impairment globally. Specifically, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, mild cognitive impairment, cerebrovascular diseases, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder were included in the review; other pathologies that can also cause cognitive impairment such as multiple sclerosis, traumatic brain injury, brain tumors, infectious diseases, and psychiatric conditions such as schizophrenia or autism spectrum disorder, or drug or toxin-related causes were outside the scope of the present review. Across the literature, studies have reported that BCI cognitive training can improve cognition performance for mild cognitive impairment, stroke, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, showcasing its feasibility as a complementary therapy. However, the amount of evidence is still scarce, with few reported randomized controlled clinical trials and all of the applications comprising non-invasive systems using electroencephalography, while invasive or other non-invasive approaches remain largely unassessed. Therefore, further research regarding the design of BCIs for targeting specific cognitive domains is necessary to allow for the future introduction of these types of systems into clinical rehabilitation environments, rather than only demonstrating their feasibility, as has been mainly done to date.

titre: The application of square-stepping exercise in patients with stroke: a scoping review.
titre_fr: The application of square-stepping exercise in patients with stroke: a scoping review.
auteurs: Yan Yali, Xu Juan, Yao Jiaxin, Liu Yuanyuan, Li Mengdan, Geng Xinxin
resume: Square-stepping exercise (SSE) is a form of dual-task training that has been used in studies involving patients with stroke. This scoping review provides an overview of the intervention protocols and outcomes reported in studies examining the use of SSE among patients with stroke. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, The Cochrane Library, CINAHL, CNKI, SinoMed, Wanfang Data, and the VIP Database were searched for studies published from 2006, when the first study on SSE was published, to April 30, 2026. A total of 459 records were identified, of which seven met the eligibility criteria and were included in the final analysis. A total of seven studies were included. The intervention types included face-to-face and hybrid interventions. The duration of a single session was generally 30 min, the frequency was mostly 3-5 times per week, and the intervention period ranged from 6 to 24 weeks. The outcome measures primarily covered two domains: motor function and cognitive function. The findings suggested that SSE may improve balance and gait function in patients with stroke and may reduce the risk of falls. In addition, SSE may improve global cognitive function, including executive function and attention. SSE may help improve motor and cognitive function in patients with stroke, but related research remains at an exploratory stage. Future research should include large-scale, multicenter studies with long-term follow-up to further clarify its long-term effects and optimal intervention protocol, explore remotely delivered SSE interventions, and promote the standardized implementation and dissemination of SSE in stroke rehabilitation.

titre: Empowering safer mobility behaviour for fall prevention in people with Parkinson's disease: A qualitative study.
titre_fr: Empowering safer mobility behaviour for fall prevention in people with Parkinson's disease: A qualitative study.
auteurs: Cheung Daniel, Paul Serene S, Mackenzie Lynette, Wesson Jacqueline, Allen Natalie E
resume: ObjectiveTo understand the perspectives of clinicians and researchers on the nature of safer mobility behaviour and how it is applied to fall prevention in people with Parkinson's disease.DesignA qualitative study using focus group discussions with reflexive thematic analysis.SettingAn international cohort participated in the study online via video conference.ParticipantsNineteen physiotherapists, occupational therapists and/or researchers (median 18 years of experience) were included across five focus groups.ResultsEmpowerment was the central theme underpinning the promotion of safer mobility behaviour. Empowerment meant enabling people towards safe, effective and meaningful task engagement. This was embedded across three sub-themes. Firstly, a contextual approach was needed to understand the complex nature of mobility behaviour involving the combination of physical, cognitive, psychological and Parkinson's disease (e.g. disease progression and fluctuations) related influences. Secondly, an individual approach was needed to provide a holistic assessment evaluating the impact of these influences as well as tailoring interventions to address them. Thirdly, a collaborative approach was needed between clinicians, individuals and care-partners to ensure shared problem solving and goal setting.ConclusionsA novel approach to fall prevention was described in this study. It recognised a person's autonomy and dignity of risk through a balanced consideration of safety during meaningful activities. It also highlighted the role of expert clinicians to work alongside individuals and care-partners for safer strategy development. This study provides the foundation for the development and implementation of safer mobility behaviour strategies for fall prevention in people with Parkinson's disease.

titre: Inner speech and the architecture of social cognition: A commentary on Silvanto (2026).
titre_fr: Inner speech and the architecture of social cognition: A commentary on Silvanto (2026).
auteurs: Geva Sharon, Lœvenbruck Hélène
revue: Cortex; a journal devoted to the study of the nervous system and behavior
resume: This commentary builds on Silvanto's (2026) argument that congenital aphantasia should be recognised as a form of cognitive diversity rather than a pathology, with rehabilitation targeting underlying causes of imagery loss rather than the restoration of mental imagery. Silvanto further highlights the association between visual imagery loss and emotional dysregulation. While we support this move away from pathologising aphantasia, we highlight a critical gap in the literature: the underappreciated role of inner speech in social-emotional cognition. We argue that sensory imagery (and aphantasia) should be recognized as a multifaceted process, with dissociations observed across modalities. Furthermore, we propose that inner speech, whether condensed or expanded (accompanied by auditory verbal imagery), serves as a computationally efficient, resource-light alternative to sensory imagery, supporting cognition without the need for detailed sensorimotor simulation. This perspective reframes aphantasia as cognitive diversity and highlights the need for greater empirical and theoretical focus on inner speech.

titre: Artificial intelligence in upper-limb, language and cognitive neurorehabilitation after stroke.
titre_fr: Artificial intelligence in upper-limb, language and cognitive neurorehabilitation after stroke.
auteurs: Hill Annie, Bauer Christoph Michael, Leochico Carl Froilan
resume: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being increasingly integrated into upper-limb, language and cognitive neurorehabilitation research and there is interest in where the research currently lies along the pipeline towards clinical implementation and real-world impact. Across these three domains of neurorehabilitation, the research into the use of AI has shown clear potential to enhance assessment, personalize rehabilitation and extend access to care but is yet to demonstrate clinical utility and superiority over other digital rehabilitation approaches. There remain concerns about small and selective datasets being used for modelling, privacy and equity issues and sustainable implementation. It is suggested that AI should be positioned as an important tool in the clinical infrastructure rather than an autonomous clinical decision maker within clinical practice. Future research across these neurorehabilitation domains should consider implementation risks and needs early in the research pipeline, by using ethical principles and guidelines to ensure transparency and consumer involvement in AI research and implementation into clinical practice.

titre: Neuroendocrine dysfunction after TBI: A guide for the clinical neuropsychologist.
titre_fr: Neuroendocrine dysfunction after TBI: A guide for the clinical neuropsychologist.
auteurs: Howell Stefanie N, Masel Brent E
resume: This review aims to provide neuropsychologists with a comprehensive understanding of neuroendocrine dysfunction following traumatic brain injury (TBI), emphasizing post-traumatic hypopituitarism (PTHP) and its implications for cognitive function and rehabilitation. A critical review of current literature on neuroendocrine dysfunction following TBI, including studies on pituitary function, hormone deficiencies, and their effects on cognition, mood, and fatigue. The review integrates findings from endocrinology, neuroscience, and clinical neuropsychology to highlight the importance of interdisciplinary management. Research indicates that a high proportion of moderate to severe TBI cases may develop PTHP, with growth hormone deficiency (GHD) as the most prevalent dysfunction. While less extensively studied, evidence suggests that individuals with persistent post-mild TBI symptoms may exhibit neuroendocrine dysfunction at similar rates to moderate to severe TBI patients. The impact of hormonal dysregulation on cognition and neuropsychological performance underscores the need for targeted assessment and intervention. Emerging data also suggest that metabolic disturbances, such as altered gut microbiota and amino acid imbalances, may contribute to post-TBI fatigue and cognitive impairment. Neuropsychologists play a vital role in identifying and referring patients with suspected neuroendocrine dysfunction for appropriate testing and treatment. Recognizing PTHP as a potential contributor to chronic TBI symptoms may lead to improved patient outcomes through targeted hormonal therapies and interdisciplinary rehabilitation strategies. Increased awareness of the relationship between TBI, pituitary dysfunction, and cognition is essential for optimizing clinical care.

titre: Psoas Atrophy Following Lateral Lumbar Interbody Fusion: A Retrospective Case Series.
titre_fr: Psoas Atrophy Following Lateral Lumbar Interbody Fusion: A Retrospective Case Series.
auteurs: Rusu Daniel, Sun Kevin, Yoshida Brandon, Lindgren Aidan R, Avetisian Henry, Karakash William J, Abdou Marc A, Wang Jeffrey C, Hah Raymond J, Alluri Ram K
revue: HSS journal : the musculoskeletal journal of Hospital for Special Surgery
resume: The direct muscular trauma caused by the trans-psoas approach of a lateral lumbar interbody fusion (LLIF) is a potential reason for its high rates of postoperative psoas weakness. We sought to compare preoperative and postoperative psoas muscle parameters to evaluate iatrogenic psoas atrophy following LLIF. We conducted a retrospective case series including patients who underwent primary LLIF at a single tertiary academic center between 2012 and 2024. Exclusion criteria included history of spinal deformity, spine surgery, neuromuscular disorders, or LLIF indicated for infection or malignancy. Participants had both preoperative and postoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans; the latter were obtained at least 3 months postoperatively. Psoas muscle atrophy was assessed using MRI measurements of cross-sectional area (CSA), anteroposterior (AP) and mediolateral diameters, and Goutallier classification for fatty infiltration. Paired and Welch's t-tests compared postoperative to preoperative and contralateral values. Subgroup analysis compared patients with and without postoperative hip flexor weakness. Forty patients met inclusion criteria (mean follow-up: 25 months). The ipsilateral psoas demonstrated significant reduction in CSA (-117 vs -22.7 mm2) and AP diameter (-2.43 vs 0.34 mm) compared with the contralateral side. Six patients (15%) had persistent hip flexor weakness. On multivariate analysis, male sex and body mass index (BMI) were risk factors for psoas atrophy. Diabetes and length of stay predicted postoperative hip flexor weakness. This retrospective study identified evidence of long-term ipsilateral psoas atrophy following LLIF, potentially contributing to postoperative hip flexor weakness. Male sex, BMI, diabetes, and length of hospital stay were identified as predictors of psoas atrophy or weakness, highlighting the importance of postoperative rehabilitation focusing on psoas preservation. Future studies are warranted to further evaluate potential risk factors for postoperative hip flexor weakness following LLIF. Level IV: retrospective case series.

titre: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Treatment Planning in Physical and Rehabilitation Medicine: A Systematic Review.
titre_fr: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Treatment Planning in Physical and Rehabilitation Medicine: A Systematic Review.
auteurs: Demeco Andrea, Marotta Nicola, Racinelli Andrea, Megna Marco, Pansera Bruno, Palermi Stefano, Vecchiato Marco, de Sire Alessandro, Ammendolia Antonio
revue: American journal of physical medicine & rehabilitation
resume: Individualized rehabilitation plans are crucial for maximizing clinical outcomes. Generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs), which can generate new content based on large knowledge bases, could improve personalized rehabilitation. This systematic review aimed to assess accuracy and application of LLMs in rehabilitation. A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus until February 2026. The PICO included LLMs (P), their use in rehabilitation planning (I), comparison with expert opinion or other AI systems (e.g., machine learning, deep learning, or CDSS) (C), the ability to generate appropriate rehabilitation plans and compliance with expert clinicians or clinical practice guidelines (O). Studies involving non-generative AI were excluded. Methodological quality was assessed with JBI tools. Data extraction was performed by two reviewers; a third resolved conflicts. Nine studies met inclusion criteria. Concordance with expert opinion varied, reaching 98.75% after an expert advisory board reviewed AI-generated statements. In musculoskeletal and cardiovascular rehabilitation, LLMs demonstrated alignment with guidelines. However, the included studies reported hallucinations, underscoring the necessity of supervision. LLMs showed promising capabilities in supporting rehabilitation treatment planning, possibly offering adaptability and personalization. Nonetheless, high-quality studies are necessary to validate real-world effectiveness and define implementation strategies.

titre: Application of Electrical Impedance Tomography-Guided Pulmonary Rehabilitation Strategy in Patients with Respiratory Failure.
titre_fr: Application of Electrical Impedance Tomography-Guided Pulmonary Rehabilitation Strategy in Patients with Respiratory Failure.
auteurs: Peng Jiangqiong, Jiang Jing, Xiao Yuting, Huang Juan, Tang Xiaoling
resume: This study investigated pulmonary rehabilitation strategies guided by electrical impedance tomography (EIT) in patients with respiratory failure. A total of 92 patients with respiratory failure admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) of a tertiary Grade A hospital in Chongqing from July 2024 to January 2025 were selected and randomly divided into a control group and an experimental group, with 46 cases in each group, using a random number table. The control group received conventional pulmonary physical therapy nursing strategies. The experimental group additionally received EIT-guided positioning, vibratory sputum clearance, and early mobilization. Relative regional tidal-ventilation distribution, PaO₂/FiO₂, respiratory rate, and pulse oxygen saturation were assessed at baseline and on the following three days; ICU stay, and delirium incidence were also compared. Finally, 44 cases in the control group and 44 cases in the experimental group completed the study. Repeated-measures ANOVA showed significant time effects across the four ventral-to-dorsal layers and significant group and interaction effects for the dorsal layer. Dorsal ventilation share was higher in the experimental group on days 2 and 3, but not significantly different on day 1. No significant group, time, or interaction effects were found for the four lung quadrants. The experimental group had higher PaO₂/FiO₂, shorter ICU stay (6.55 vs. 7.75 days), and lower delirium incidence (25.0% vs. 45.5%). Respiratory rate decreased, and pulse oxygen saturation increased over time in both groups, without significant group or interaction effects. The EIT-guided strategy may improve regional ventilation distribution and oxygenation, shorten ICU stay, and reduce delirium in patients with respiratory failure.

titre: Current Evidence of Rehabilitation for Patients with Drug-resistant Epilepsy: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
titre_fr: Current Evidence of Rehabilitation for Patients with Drug-resistant Epilepsy: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
auteurs: Inaba Tasuku, Hara Takatoshi, Matsunaga Ayaka, Miyazaki Yuta, Kawaguchi Taiyo, Yamaguchi Takashi, Iwasaki Masaki, Iijima Keiya, Yoshida Kentaro, Abo Masahiro
resume: Drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) affects 20%-30% of individuals with epilepsy and is associated with persistent seizures, cognitive and psychosocial impairments, and reduced health-related quality of life (HRQoL). Although surgery and neuromodulation are established non-pharmacological options, the role of rehabilitation remains unclear. This systematic review synthesized evidence on rehabilitation for DRE and aimed to clarify its clinical relevance in terms of seizure, motor, cognitive, and quality-of-life outcomes. Five databases (PubMed, CENTRAL, CINAHL, PEDro, and ProQuest) were searched for studies published between January 2015 and March 2025. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), controlled clinical trials, and observational studies in patients with DRE receiving rehabilitation. The outcomes included seizure frequency, cognitive function, HRQoL, psychological health, and physical function. The methodological quality of RCTs was assessed using the PEDro scale. A narrative synthesis was performed, and meta-analyses of studies on physical exercise therapy were conducted to compare outcomes. Eleven studies met the criteria: four RCTs, one non-RCT, and six observational studies. The interventions included physical exercise therapy (n = 4), postoperative rehabilitation after anterior temporal lobe resection or hemispherotomy (n = 4), neuropsychological rehabilitation (n = 1), monitoring daily activities (n = 1), and a qualitative study (n = 1). Meta-analyses of RCTs found no significant effects of exercise therapy on seizure frequency or HRQoL. DRE rehabilitation is multifaceted and encompasses exercises, cognitive training, and postoperative rehabilitation. Exercise therapy appears safe; however, the effects on seizure control and HRQoL are inconclusive. The limited evidence in DRE rehabilitation underscores the need for larger, methodologically rigorous trials with standardized outcomes.

The outcomes included seizure frequency, cognitive function, HRQoL, psychological health, and physical function. The methodological quality of RCTs was assessed using the PEDro scale. A narrative synthesis was performed, and meta-analyses of studies on physical exercise therapy were conducted to compare outcomes. Eleven studies met the criteria: four RCTs, one non-RCT, and six observational studies. The interventions included physical exercise therapy (n = 4), postoperative rehabilitation after anterior temporal lobe resection or hemispherotomy (n = 4), neuropsychological rehabilitation (n = 1), monitoring daily activities (n = 1), and a qualitative study (n = 1). Meta-analyses of RCTs found no significant effects of exercise therapy on seizure frequency or HRQoL. DRE rehabilitation is multifaceted and encompasses exercises, cognitive training, and postoperative rehabilitation. Exercise therapy appears safe; however, the effects on seizure control and HRQoL are inconclusive. The limited evidence in DRE rehabilitation underscores the need for larger, methodologically rigorous trials with standardized outcomes.

titre: Optimising methodology, biomechanics and imaging in biological augmentation for partial-thickness rotator cuff tears: A commentary on Demiral et al.
titre_fr: Optimising methodology, biomechanics and imaging in biological augmentation for partial-thickness rotator cuff tears: A commentary on Demiral et al.
auteurs: He Haoxiang, Shen Weidong, Tao Jiming
revue: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
resume: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) combined with physical therapy (PT) represents a growing paradigm in the nonoperative management of partial-thickness rotator cuff tears (PTRCTs). In a recent publication in Knee Surgery, Sports Traumatology, Arthroscopy, Demiral et al. reported significant clinical and radiological improvements following PRP supplementation in articular-sided partial supraspinatus tears. While their findings provide encouragement for biologic augmentation, several methodological nuances warrant deeper examination. This commentary provides a broader critical perspective on three essential domains: baseline functional comparability and statistical model selection, the biological-biomechanical interface during early rehabilitation loading, and radiological precision in magnetic resonance arthrography (MRA) tear volume estimation. By addressing these methodological challenges, we aim to offer actionable guidance for future clinical trial designs and therapeutic protocols in sports medicine and orthopaedic rehabilitation. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: NA.

titre: Exercise-based rehabilitation interventions for kinesiophobia after total knee arthroplasty: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
titre_fr: Exercise-based rehabilitation interventions for kinesiophobia after total knee arthroplasty: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
auteurs: Wen Hongbo, Zhang Ting, Xie Tingting, Xue Huiqin
resume: Affecting 21-35% of patients after total knee arthroplasty (TKA), kinesiophobia critically impedes postoperative rehabilitation. Whether exercise-based interventions reduce kinesiophobia more effectively than routine postoperative rehabilitation remains unclear. We systematically searched 11 databases from inception to July 11, 2026, for RCTs comparing exercise-based rehabilitation with routine postoperative rehabilitation in adults undergoing primary TKA. The primary outcome was kinesiophobia. Secondary outcomes included knee function, pain, balance, mobilization time, and adherence. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed using RevMan 5.4. Certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE. Eleven RCTs (N = 1,096) were included. Exercise-based rehabilitation was associated with a reduction in kinesiophobia (SMD = - 1.22, 95% CI [- 1.72, - 0.72]; I<sup>2</sup> = 93%; low certainty) and improvements in knee function (SMD = 1.19, 95% CI [0.67, 1.71]; I<sup>2</sup> = 93%; low certainty). For pain, the ≤ 4-week pooled estimate (SMD = - 1.09, 95% CI [- 2.03, - 0.14]; I<sup>2</sup> = 94%) was not interpretable due to extreme heterogeneity and was not robust: after exclusion of the single acute in-hospital trial, the confidence interval crossed zero (SMD = - 1.09, 95% CI [- 2.28, 0.09]). Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses otherwise supported the directional conclusions for kinesiophobia and knee function, although effect sizes were unstable and certainty remained low. Low-certainty evidence suggests that exercise-based rehabilitation may be associated with reductions in kinesiophobia at ≤ 4 weeks and an interpretable 12-week improvement in knee function after TKA; the ≤ 4-week and ≥ 24-week functional subgroup estimates were not interpretable because of extreme heterogeneity, and the early pain signal was possible but non-robust. Effect sizes should be interpreted with caution due to substantial heterogeneity, risk of bias, and sensitivity to outlying studies. Well-designed, multicenter RCTs with rigorous blinding and standardized protocols are urgently needed.

titre: Early Versus Delayed Rehabilitation Following First Metatarsophalangeal Joint Implant Arthroplasty: A Retrospective Comparison of 40 Cases.
titre_fr: Early Versus Delayed Rehabilitation Following First Metatarsophalangeal Joint Implant Arthroplasty: A Retrospective Comparison of 40 Cases.
auteurs: Głodkowska-Sutuła Jagoda, Świerkowski Igor
revue: The Journal of foot and ankle surgery : official publication of the American College of Foot and Ankle Surgeons
resume: First metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint implant arthroplasty is used to preserve joint mobility and reduce pain in patients with advanced hallux rigidus. The optimal timing of postoperative rehabilitation remains unclear. To compare clinical outcomes associated with early versus delayed rehabilitation following first MTP joint implant arthroplasty. Retrospective comparative study. Forty patients who underwent first MTP joint implant arthroplasty were analyzed. Twenty initiated rehabilitation immediately after suture removal (mean, 2.1 ± 0.4 weeks after surgery), whereas 20 initiated rehabilitation later (mean, 21.4 ± 3.0 weeks after surgery). Both groups followed the same standardized rehabilitation protocol. Outcomes assessed before and after rehabilitation included dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, pain intensity using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS), and the AOFAS Hallux Score. Group × Time interactions were evaluated using mixed-design ANOVA and linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age and sex. Greater improvements were observed in the early rehabilitation group for dorsiflexion (+12.35° vs +6.75°), plantarflexion (+4.70° vs +1.70°), VAS (-3.35 vs -1.50), and AOFAS score (+26.90 vs +11.00). Significant Group × Time interactions were found for all outcomes (p ≤ 0.001), and the associations remained significant after adjustment for age and sex. Early rehabilitation was associated with greater improvements in joint mobility, pain, and functional outcomes than delayed rehabilitation. Given the retrospective, nonrandomized design and differences in postoperative assessment timing, these findings should be interpreted cautiously and confirmed in prospective studies. III (Retrospective comparative study).

titre: Effects of blood flow restriction therapy on lower-limb strength in multiple sclerosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
titre_fr: Effects of blood flow restriction therapy on lower-limb strength in multiple sclerosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
auteurs: Blanco-Trillo Andrea, Mollinedo-Cardalda Irimia, Guerra-Colmenero Claudia, Fernández-Vázquez Diego
resume: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic neurodegenerative disease that impairs muscle strength, gait, and functional capacity. Blood flow restriction (BFR) therapy has emerged as a promising low-load rehabilitation strategy, although evidence in people with MS (pwMS) remains limited and heterogeneous. To analyze the current scientific evidence regarding the effects of BFR therapy on lower-limb muscle strength in pwMS. PRISMA-based review included a systematic search of eight electronic databases. Clinical and quasi-experimental studies involving people with MS that evaluated lower-limb BFR interventions were included, with lower-limb muscle strength as the primary outcome. The primary outcome for meta-analysis was de standardized mean differences (SMD) in strength. Methodological quality and risk of bias were assessed using the PEDro, JBI scales, RoB 2 and ROBINS-I V2 tools. Five studies met the inclusion criteria. Interventions ranged from 6 to 12 weeks with low training loads (30-40% of one-repetition maximum) and occlusion pressures ranging from 30% to 80% of arterial occlusion pressure. Compared with exercise alone, exercise combined with BFR significantly improved quadriceps (SMD=-0.55) and hamstring strength (SMD=-0.38), and possibly reduced fatigue (SMD=-0.35), with low heterogeneity across analyses. However, the statistical significance of the effect on quadriceps strength was lost in the sensitivity analysis. Methodological quality and overall risk of bias varied from moderate to good. BFR therapy may improve lower-limb strength (more consistently for hamstrings than quadriceps) and may reduce fatigue in people with MS compared with exercise alone, but the certainty of the evidence is low. The quadriceps effect was not robust to sensitivity analysis, and no clear benefit was found for sit-to-stand or gait outcomes. The evidence does not allow conclusions on equivalence to high-load training or on optimal occlusion pressure or intervention duration. Lager, high-quality randomized trials are needed.

titre: Effects of eye movement exercise combined with conventional physical therapy on chronic nonspecific neck pain: a randomized controlled trial protocol.
titre_fr: Effects of eye movement exercise combined with conventional physical therapy on chronic nonspecific neck pain: a randomized controlled trial protocol.
auteurs: Gou Li, Yu Shiya, Wang Zhuo, Kang Yuan, Hou Yue, Yang Lin
revue: Frontiers in sports and active living
resume: Chronic nonspecific neck pain (CNNP) is a prevalent and disabling musculoskeletal disorder frequently accompanied by cervical sensorimotor deficits and autonomic nervous system (ANS) dysregulation while conventional physical therapy (CPT) can reduce pain and disability, its effects are often limited in autonomic nerve system dysfunction. Eye movement exercise (EME) engages oculomotor-vestibular-proprioceptive networks and stimulates vagal-parasympathetic pathways, offering potential synergistic benefits. However, clinical evidence supporting an EME-integrated rehabilitation regimen in CNNP is scarce. This trial aims to evaluate the efficacy of EME + CPT compared to CPT alone on relieving pain intensity, disability intensity, autonomic regulation, and quality of life for CNNP. A single-centre, assessor-blinded randomized controlled trial will recruit 60 adults with CNNP ≥12 weeks. Participants will be randomly assigned (1:1) to either CPT alone or CPT + EME group. Interventions will be administered three times per week for four consecutive weeks (about 60 min per session). The primary outcome is pain intensity (measured using a 100-mm visual analogue scale, VAS). The prespecified primary endpoint is Day 30, and the primary treatment contrast is the between-group difference in mean change in VAS from baseline to Day 30. Secondary outcomes include neck disability index, cervical active range of motion, anxiety and depression severity and health-related quality of life. Heart rate variability (HRV) is prespecified as a secondary mechanistic outcome, whereas oculomotor performance and electrical sensory/pain thresholds, and eye movement accuracy are exploratory outcomes. Data will be collected at baseline, Day 15, and Day 30. The primary analysis will use a linear mixed-effects model under the intention-to-treat principle. This trial will clarify whether integrating structured EME into a standard rehabilitation framework confers incremental short-term clinical benefits over conventional therapy of equal total duration. Exploratory autonomic and oculomotor endpoints will provide insight into underlying physiological associations rather than inferring direct causality, informing future large-scale, long-term rehabilitation trials. https://www.chictr.org.cn/bin/project/edit?pid=293180, identifier ChiCTR2500111782.

titre: Effect of Incorporating Perceptual Learning Into Plantar Hardness Discrimination on the Risk of Falling and Muscle Torque in Patients With Hemiplegia: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
titre_fr: Effect of Incorporating Perceptual Learning Into Plantar Hardness Discrimination on the Risk of Falling and Muscle Torque in Patients With Hemiplegia: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
auteurs: Mahmoud Lama Saad El-Din, Mohamed Hanaa S, Shafeek Marian M, Mahmud Mohammed Saad El-Din, M Battesha Hanan Hosny
revue: American journal of physical medicine & rehabilitation
resume: This study aims to evaluate the impact of perceptual training involving plantar hardness discrimination on fall risk and muscle torque in individuals with hemiplegia. A randomized controlled trial was conducted in thirty-four stroke patients were randomly assigned to the study and control groups in equal numbers and assessed both before and after treatment. The outcome evaluations comprised fall risk assessment by the Biodex Balance System (BBS), the Isokinetic assessment of lower-limb muscle torque, and the Functional Independent Measures Scale (FIM). Each group was given a selected physical treatment program, while the study group also received perceptual learning with plantar hardness discrimination. Post-treatment comparison revealed that the study group exhibited a significantly lower risk of falling than the control group (P <0.001, effect size [ES]=1.48). Similarly, knee extensors torque increased significantly in the study group relative to the control group (P <0.001, ES=1.19). Additionally, the study group showed a significant rise in FIM scores compared with the control group (P <0.001, ES=1.56). For stroke patients, incorporating perceptual learning into plantar hardness discrimination in the rehabilitation program is regarded as beneficial physical therapy neurorehabilitation for enhancing risk of falling, lower limb muscle torque and function.

titre: Effects of exercise-based interventions on balance and functional mobility in adults with chronic stroke: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
titre_fr: Effects of exercise-based interventions on balance and functional mobility in adults with chronic stroke: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
auteurs: Zhan Yating, Bai Hao, Pan Tongtong, Li Yue, Wang Rong
resume: To systematically evaluate, using the GRADE framework, the effects of exercise-based interventions on Berg Balance Scale, Timed Up and Go, and Functional Reach Test outcomes in adults with chronic stroke. We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Physiotherapy Evidence Database from inception to 29 June 2025 for randomized controlled trials investigating structured exercise-based interventions in adults with chronic stroke. Eligible studies enrolled adults at least 6 months after stroke onset and reported at least one validated balance or functional mobility outcome. Methodological quality was assessed using the Physiotherapy Evidence Database scale, and the certainty of evidence was rated using the GRADE approach. Meta-analyses were performed using random-effects models and expressed as mean differences (MDs) or standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs); exploratory univariable random-effects meta-regression was used to examine intervention duration and training frequency. Sixty-nine randomized controlled trials involving 2,314 adults with chronic stroke were included. Exercise-based interventions improved Berg Balance Scale scores [MD = 2.54, 95% CI (1.83-3.26)], reduced Timed Up and Go test completion time [MD = -2.68 s, 95% CI (-3.72 to -1.65)], and improved Functional Reach Test performance [SMD = 0.65, 95% CI (0.25-1.05)]. The certainty of evidence was moderate for BBS, high for TUG, and moderate for FRT, with the degree of heterogeneity differing across outcomes. Exercise-based interventions were associated with improvements in BBS scores, TUG performance, and FRT outcomes in adults with chronic stroke, although the certainty and consistency of evidence varied across these measures. These findings support the potential role of exercise-based interventions in improving these selected outcomes. Larger pragmatic trials with standardized intervention reporting and longer follow-up are needed to clarify optimal training components, dose, delivery, and durability of effects. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42020156992, identifier CRD42020156992.

titre: Therapeutic Ultrasound for Pain Management in Temporomandibular Disorders: A Systematic Review of Clinical Evidence From Controlled and Prospective Studies.
titre_fr: Therapeutic Ultrasound for Pain Management in Temporomandibular Disorders: A Systematic Review of Clinical Evidence From Controlled and Prospective Studies.
auteurs: Zhou Xiaofeng, Wang Dawei, Jiang Feng, Liu Hui, Wang Junyan
resume: Temporomandibular disorders (TMDs) are a common source of persistent orofacial pain and are estimated to affect a substantial proportion of the population. Therapeutic ultrasound is a non-invasive modality frequently used in musculoskeletal rehabilitation, although its clinical effectiveness for TMD-related pain remains debated. This systematic review was designed and reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 recommendations. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from database inception to April 2026. We included randomized controlled trials, prospective clinical studies, and comparative clinical designs evaluating therapeutic ultrasound for pain management in adults with TMDs. The primary outcomes were pain intensity, assessed using VAS, NRS, or VRS, and mandibular function, assessed mainly by mouth opening. Risk of bias was evaluated using the Cochrane RoB 2.0 tool for randomized trials and ROBINS-I for non-randomized studies. Because of substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively rather than pooled statistically. The search identified 143 records, of which 82 remained after duplicate removal and were screened. Thirty-seven full-text articles were assessed, and 23 studies involving 1256 participants (1226 of them with a temporomandibular disorder) met the eligibility criteria. Twenty-one of 23 studies reported a statistically significant reduction in pain relative to their own baseline; however, these are within-group changes rather than treatment effects, and the certainty of the evidence for pain reduction was very low (GRADE), with low certainty for mandibular function, pressure pain threshold and quality of life/disability. Reported reductions included VAS improvement from 42 to 18 when ultrasound was added to home exercise, compared with 40-26 with exercise alone, and VAS improvement from 4.90 to 1.70 after low-intensity ultrasound therapy in a large randomized trial. Compared with low-level laser therapy or photobiomodulation, four studies favored laser-based treatment, whereas one study favored low-intensity ultrasound combined with exercise. Ultrasound was superior to TENS in two studies, while one study found no meaningful difference among ultrasound, TENS, and LLLT. No consistent difference was observed between continuous and pulsed ultrasound modes. Among randomized trials, 8 studies were judged as low risk of bias, 8 raised some concerns, and 1 was judged as high risk of bias. Adverse events were reported by only 2 of the 23 studies, so the safety of the intervention could not be characterised. Therapeutic ultrasound may reduce pain and improve mandibular function in patients with temporomandibular disorders, particularly as an adjunct to multimodal rehabilitation; however, the certainty of the evidence is very low for pain and low for mandibular function, pressure pain threshold and quality of life/disability, and the optimal treatment parameters remain undetermined. These findings should not be interpreted as establishing clinical efficacy. Although some comparative studies reported greater pain reduction with LLLT/PBM than with ultrasound, this finding should be interpreted cautiously because the number of studies was small and treatment protocols were heterogeneous. Therefore, current evidence does not establish the superiority of LLLT/PBM over therapeutic ultrasound.
