titre: The integrated bioenergetic-interoceptive model of schizophrenia-spectrum disorders.
titre_fr: The integrated bioenergetic-interoceptive model of schizophrenia-spectrum disorders.
auteurs: Szendi István, Treuer Tamás
resume: Schizophrenia has traditionally been conceptualized as a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental disorder involving neurotransmitter dysregulation, synaptic dysfunction, and large-scale brain network abnormalities. However, a growing body of convergent evidence indicates that schizophrenia is embedded in broader, system-level physiological dysregulation involving metabolic, immune, endocrine, gastrointestinal, autonomic, and interoceptive alterations. This article proposes an integrated bioenergetic-interoceptive model of schizophrenia-spectrum disorders, in which the disorder is understood as a disturbance of predictive allostatic regulation under energetic constraint. According to the model, reduced metabolic flexibility, altered cerebral bioenergetics, cumulative allostatic load, microbiome-gut-brain axis dysregulation, and disturbed interoceptive timing converge on late-maturing, energetically demanding association networks that support salience attribution, self-referential processing, cognitive control, social cognition, and embodied self-experience. Within this framework, the mismatch between energy demand and available capacity constitutes a functionally proximal energetic constraint on adaptive brain-body regulation, whereas impaired metabolic flexibility represents one possible dynamic mechanism underlying this constraint. Gut-immune-metabolite signaling is interpreted as a modulatory input system that may alter the reliability and metabolic cost of interoceptive inference. Gastric, cardiac, respiratory, and vagal rhythms may constitute candidate timing mechanisms through which bodily signals contribute to the temporal organization of the embodied self. The model further posits that neotenous association cortical systems and large-scale networks-including the default mode, salience, frontoparietal, cingulo-insular, and self-referential systems-are particularly vulnerable to convergent metabolic, inflammatory, autonomic, and interoceptive stressors. The model reframes schizophrenia as a multisystem disturbance of predictive brain-body regulation and delineates testable directions for future multimodal biomarker research and for adjunctive interventions targeting bioenergetic, inflammatory, autonomic, gut-brain, and interoceptive mechanisms.

titre: Case Report: A novel hemizygous nonsense variant in PPP1R3F gene associated with developmental delay, intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder.
titre_fr: Case Report: A novel hemizygous nonsense variant in PPP1R3F gene associated with developmental delay, intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder.
auteurs: Yang Qi, Zhang Qinle, Zhang Qiang, Zhou Xunzhao, Yi Shang, Qin Zailong, He Sheng, Luo Jingsi
resume: PPP1R3F deficiency syndrome is an extremely rare, recently identified X-linked recessive neurodevelopmental disorder. It is caused by hemizygous variants in the PPP1R3F gene, which encodes a glycogen-targeting subunit of the brain-specific protein phosphatase 1 (PP1). Dysfunction of PPP1R3F disrupts glycogen metabolism in astrocytes, leading to insufficient energy supply to synapses during critical periods of brain development and subsequently causing neurodevelopmental abnormalities. Only a small number of cases of PPP1R3F deficiency syndrome have been reported to date, which significantly limits our comprehensive understanding of the clinical features of the disease and the relationship between genetic variants and clinical manifestations in patients. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was performed on a Chinese male presenting with intellectual disability (ID), developmental delay (DD), and autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Sanger sequencing was then used to identify and determine the origins of the variant. We evaluated the pathogenicity of the identified variant following the established ACMG/AMP guidelines. Additionally, we conducted a thorough review of previously reported cases to summarize the variants and clinical features of PPP1R3F deficiency syndrome. We identified a novel hemizygous nonsense variant [NM_033215.5: c.907C>T, p.(Gln303*)] in the PPP1R3F gene in the proband, which was inherited from his mother. The patient we described here exhibited clinical phenotypes similar to those associated with PPP1R3F gene variants but lacked other reported multisystem manifestations, such as epilepsy, brain abnormalities, and dysmorphic features. An analysis of the 15 variants and their associated phenotypes in 15 patients from both the current and previous studies demonstrates that PPP1R3F gene variants can lead to a variety of phenotypic deficits, and a clear genotype-phenotype correlation has not yet been established. Despite the high variability in some clinical manifestations, the core phenotypic features of PPP1R3F variants include varying degrees of ID, DD, speech delay, dysmorphic facial features, and ASD. Our findings support DD, ID, ASD, and speech impairment as core features of PPP1R3F deficiency syndrome, while also highlighting the extensive clinical variability. This study further expanded the genetic and phenotypic spectrum associated with PPP1R3F deficiency syndrome.

Our findings support DD, ID, ASD, and speech impairment as core features of PPP1R3F deficiency syndrome, while also highlighting the extensive clinical variability. This study further expanded the genetic and phenotypic spectrum associated with PPP1R3F deficiency syndrome.

titre: Convergent molecular pathways and shared genetic mechanisms in classic syndromic autism spectrum disorders: a narrative review.
titre_fr: Convergent molecular pathways and shared genetic mechanisms in classic syndromic autism spectrum disorders: a narrative review.
auteurs: Bourgaize Ryan, Oyetunji Aderonke, Butler Merlin G
resume: Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) are defined as a group of neurodevelopmental disorders that share common core features including restrictive repetitive stereotypic behavioral patterns and interests affecting social communication. Over 1,200 genes have been associated with ASD and impacted by copy number variants, chromosomal, and/or single gene defects or epigenetics. Genetic factors contribute to most cases of autism. At least twelve classic genetic disorders with autism as a common feature were selected involving 31 causative or implicated genes with 30 recognized as ASD genes. These disorders were selected to represent a range of genetic abnormalities such as chromosomal deletions, duplications, or trisomy, as well as single or multiple defective genes often with inter-relationship to other genes. Collectively, these syndromes present with neurodevelopmental/behavior/psychiatric findings with ASD, ADHD, intellectual disability and/or psychosis as features. This narrative review is novel by synthesizing available evidence on shared genes, molecular pathways, and protein-protein interaction networks across twelve classic syndromic autism spectrum disorders. Drawing on existing literature and curated web-based databases including STRING and BioGRID, nineteen of the 31 causative and/or implicated genes identified across syndromic autism disorders showed overlap across the twelve classic syndromes having different genetic defects and converged on shared molecular functions, pathways and biological processes. These related to chromatin remodeling, RNA regulation of neurodevelopment and function, synaptic signaling, neuronal connectivity, and protein homeostasis. Phelan-McDermid, Fragile X, Rett, Prader-Willi, Angelman, Burnside-Butler, and Cornelia de Lange syndromes exhibited overlapping pathways related to typical features of autism including social behavior, language acquisition, and associated neurodevelopment. Novel observations of shared molecular patterns across classic genetically distinct syndromes with ASD showed disturbances suggestive of unified, pathway-based therapeutics requiring more investigations to inform future treatment strategies.

titre: International Multicenter Retrospective Study on UBTF-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder.
titre_fr: International Multicenter Retrospective Study on UBTF-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder.
auteurs: Balletto Giulia, Carli Sara, Coppola Antonietta, Torella Annalaura, Lee Hsiu-Fen, Korenke Christoph, Lebon Sebastien, Sedlackova Lucie, Nagy Amanda, Eichler Florian S, Murali Chaya N, Nigro Vincenzo, Ladha Farah Alnoor, Ledoux Mark S, Pelle Silvia, Prato Giulia, Nobili Lino, Chiriatti Luigi, Mancini Cecilia, Zampino Giuseppe, Graziano Claudio, Baranano Kristin, Planté-Bordeneuve Pauline, Caumes Roseline, Lauerová Barbora, Haberlová Jana, Cordelli Duccio Maria, Fiorillo Chiara, Tartaglia Marco, Tinker Rory James, Garone Caterina
resume: UBTF encodes the upstream binding transcription factor (UBTF), a protein essential for rRNA synthesis. Dominantly acting pathogenic variants, either de novo or inherited, have been associated with a broad clinical childhood-onset neurodegenerative/neurodevelopmental spectrum whose genotype-phenotype correlation has not been accurately defined yet. This multicenter study aims to conduct a retrospective analysis of a large cohort of patients with pathogenic variants in the UBTF gene to refine diagnostic criteria and identify clinically relevant outcome measures for future trials. Clinical centers provided clinical, molecular, and neuroimaging data on patients carrying pathogenic or predicted pathogenic UBTF variants, consistent with the clinical phenotype. Data were collected using an human phenotype ontology-based standardized electronic case report form and included unreported cases or updated information on patients reported in the literature from January 2017 to December 2024. A cohort of 49 patients (23 previously unreported) was included in the study. The disease typically presented at ≤3 years (89.6%) with neuroregression in 71.4% of cases, either in a child with preexisting neurodevelopmental delay (42.9%) or after previously normal psychomotor development (28.6%). Less frequently, neurodevelopmental delay occurred in isolation (26.5%). During disease progression, patients developed behavioral abnormalities (81.6%), movement disorders (78.3%), autonomic manifestations (50.0%), and epilepsy (34.7%). At the last follow-up (mean age 13 years and 6 months), only 2 patients were deceased (4.1%). The main neuroimaging findings included white matter hyperintensity (68.1%), cerebral (66.0%) and cerebellar (51.1%) atrophy, and thinning of the corpus callosum (38.3%). However, brain MRI findings were reported as normal in 21.3% of cases. We identified 7 novel UBTF variants (c.271G>C; c.349A>T; c.495C>A; c.517G>A; c.761A>G; c.1048-2A>G; and c.1625_1626+15del). Genotype-phenotype analysis led to the distinction of 2 allelic, clinically distinct disorders: a childhood-onset neurodegenerative disease due to gain-of-function variants, characterized by the triad of neuroregression, movement, and behavioral disorders, and a neurodevelopmental disorder with a milder clinical course associated with loss-of-function/hypomorphic variants. The results from our deep-phenotyping analysis suggest the classification of UBTF-related disease into 2 main clinical syndromes impacting the natural history of the disease with a different degree of severity and complexity. This novel observation should be considered in the management and prognosis of patients and will be fundamental in the design of targeted therapies.

titre: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 2D in two Acadian families: functional RNA characterization of the recurrent SEPSECS c.388+3A>G variant.
titre_fr: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 2D in two Acadian families: functional RNA characterization of the recurrent SEPSECS c.388+3A>G variant.
auteurs: Bouhamdani Nadia, Fournier Raphael, Dyack Sarah, Roddick Kayla, Nikkola Elina, Chen ZhenBin, Pipko Neta, Liang Yijing, Deshwar Ashish R, Costain Gregory, Al-Younis Inas, Ben Amor Mouna
resume: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 2D (PCH2D, OMIM #613811) is an ultra-rare autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in SEPSECS, which encodes a key enzyme required for selenoprotein biosynthesis. An extensive literature review conducted for this report identified approximately 34 genetically confirmed patients from 26 families with SEPSECS-related disease across the published literature, underscoring the extreme rarity of PCH2D. Intronic splice-altering variants with functional RNA confirmation remain poorly characterized, and no population-specific founder variant has been established for SEPSECS-related PCH2D. We performed detailed clinical, molecular, and transcriptomic analyses in three affected individuals from two unrelated Acadian families originating from the Canadian Maritime provinces. All individuals underwent exome sequencing, followed by RNA-based analyses of patient-derived samples to assess the functional impact of the recurrent intronic SEPSECS variant. Exome sequencing identified the same homozygous intronic SEPSECS variant, c.388 + 3A>G, in all three affected individuals. The variant was initially classified as a variant of uncertain significance in patients 1 and 2 and as likely pathogenic in patient 3 by different diagnostic laboratories. RNA analysis demonstrated aberrant splicing with exon 3 skipping, generating an out-of-frame transcript consistent with a loss-of-function mechanism. Residual normally spliced transcript was also detected in blood-derived RNA, consistent with a partial or "leaky" splice defect at the transcript level. These findings supported pathogenic reclassification and established a molecular diagnosis of PCH2D. Clinically, the patients presented with early-onset lower-extremity spasticity, gait abnormalities, nystagmus, and mild neurodevelopmental delay, but had an attenuated clinical course compared to classical severe PCH2D. This case series expands the molecular and clinical spectrum of SEPSECS-related PCH2D by providing functional RNA evidence for a recurrent non-canonical intronic splice variant and documenting an attenuated infantile-onset presentation. The recurrence of c.388 + 3A>G in individuals of Acadian ancestry raises the possibility of a candidate Acadian founder allele. These findings underscore the importance of transcript-level analyses for interpreting intronic variants and improving diagnosis in ultra-rare neurodevelopmental disorders.

titre: Human foetal cortical slice cultures: A translational platform for studying early neurodevelopment.
titre_fr: Human foetal cortical slice cultures: A translational platform for studying early neurodevelopment.
auteurs: McLeod Faye, Dimtsi Anna, Savage Michael A, Hedley Ann, Clowry Gavin J, Trevelyan Andrew J
resume: The developing human neocortex is characterised by complex and dynamic changes in cellular architecture, neuronal organisation and activity. We previously described how human foetal cortical organotypic slice cultures, prepared from ethically sourced tissue could be used to investigate these processes. Cultures can be maintained for weeks, exhibiting features of the normal developing brain that are not replicated in current organoid models. Such cultures allow the possibility for experimental manipulation, for instance testing the effects of genetic mutations. Here we extend the characterisation of our model. We report that these organotypic cultures preserve the laminar organisation of the developing cortical wall and show considerable diversity of neuronal morphology. Employing bulk mRNA hybridisation for 794 genes (a "human neuropathology" gene panel), we identified consistent patterns of evolving gene expression between 0 and 14 days in vitro (DIV) across different tissue samples taken at 16-18 post-conceptional weeks (pcw). To put this in the context of the normal developmental pattern, we compared our data set with previously acquired tissue RNAseq data collected between 7-17 pcw (https://www.hdbr.org/expression). This indicated that many gene expression changes in vitro followed prior developmental trajectories, but others diverged strongly, including upregulated genes associated with responses to stress, and downregulated genes associated with the vascular function. This latter effect may reflect the redundancy of vascular development in culture. Notably, various genes associated with pre- and post- synaptic function, including both glutamate and GABA receptors, continued to be expressed strongly. Consistent with this, we observed spontaneous neuronal network activity in the subplate (SP) using targeted expression of the genetically encoded Ca<sup>2+</sup> indicator, GCaMPf6, to post-mitotic neurons. The frequency of neuronal Ca<sup>2+</sup> transients increased when blockers of either GABA<sub>A</sub> receptors or gap junctions were applied. Conversely, activity was significantly reduced by glutamatergic receptor antagonists and abolished by voltage gated sodium channel blockade. Neuronal Ca<sup>2+</sup> transients were triggered directly by focal application of glutamate in the SP and subventricular zone, whereas cortical plate neurons exhibited weaker responses. This was consistent with levels of immunoreactivity for glutamate receptor sub-units in these compartments. In conclusion, the organotypic cultures show functional synaptic networks, supported by continued expression of the relevant synaptic protein machinery. These data provide further validation of organotypic cultures as a model for investigating and manipulating the early prenatal development of human neocortex, a period that is otherwise difficult to study.

titre: Clinical and Economic Burdens of ADHD Across Developmental Stages: A Review.
titre_fr: Clinical and Economic Burdens of ADHD Across Developmental Stages: A Review.
auteurs: Salehpour Farzad, Gonzalez-Lima Francisco
resume: Background: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder that can persist across the lifespan and is associated with substantial clinical, economic, and psychosocial burden. This narrative review examines the clinical and economic burdens of ADHD on individuals and families, encompassing direct medical costs, including assessment and treatment expenditures, alongside non-medical costs, educational and occupational disruption, caregiving demands, and adverse mental health outcomes among family members. It synthesizes evidence across developmental stages and geographic regions and considers the clinical implications of these interconnected burdens. Methods: A structured search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase, supplemented by reference-list screening, identified English-language publications from January 2000 through June 2026. Evidence was synthesized narratively across direct medical, non-medical, and family-related burdens, prioritizing large population-based and administrative claims studies, longitudinal investigations, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses. Interpretation considered study design, confounding factors, economic perspectives, and differences in cost estimation. Results: ADHD is associated with substantial healthcare, non-medical, and family-related economic costs. Reported costs encompass diagnostic assessment, treatment, comorbidity, and adverse events, alongside educational support, occupational losses, accidents, and criminal justice involvement. Families experience reduced occupational productivity, elevated caregiving demands, greater healthcare utilization, and increased depression, anxiety, and stress. Conclusions: Clinically, these findings support assessing functional and family-level burden alongside symptoms, identifying and managing comorbidities, maintaining treatment during transitions to adult services, and monitoring tolerability. Integrating these burden domains into routine assessment and treatment planning may help identify modifiable drivers of impairment and guide more comprehensive care across the lifespan for patients and their families.

titre: Plant-Based Diets and Thyroid Homeostasis in Children and Adolescents: Balancing Anti-Inflammatory Potential and Micronutrient Vulnerability.
titre_fr: Plant-Based Diets and Thyroid Homeostasis in Children and Adolescents: Balancing Anti-Inflammatory Potential and Micronutrient Vulnerability.
auteurs: Luppino Giovanni, Franchina Francesca, Pontone Matteo, Wasniewska Malgorzata, Stagi Stefano
resume: Plant-based diets are increasingly common among children and adolescents because of their potential health benefits, environmental sustainability, and ethical considerations. However, their implications for thyroid health during growth and development remain incompletely characterised. The effects of plant-based diets on thyroid function may depend on overall diet quality and the extent of exclusion of animal-derived foods. Well-planned plant-based diets provide bioactive compounds, dietary fibre, and unsaturated fatty acids that may reduce oxidative stress and inflammation, promote a healthy gut microbiota, and support immune homeostasis. Conversely, poorly planned diets, particularly those rich in ultra-processed foods, may promote inflammation, oxidative stress, and intestinal dysbiosis. Vegetarian and vegan diet patterns may also increase the risk of inadequate intake of iodine, iron, zinc, selenium, and vitamins, while some plant-derived foods, including soy products and cruciferous vegetables, may influence thyroid physiology. These issues are particularly relevant during childhood, when thyroid hormones are essential for neurodevelopment, growth, and metabolic regulation. Current evidence suggests that thyroid health depends primarily on overall diet quality and micronutrient adequacy rather than the exclusion of animal-derived foods itself. This review critically examines these relationships, with particular emphasis on paediatric evidence.

titre: Effects of a Targeted Nutritional Intervention on Auditory-Visual Event-Related Potentials in South-Indian Infants: An Exploratory Analysis of a Cluster Randomized Trial.
titre_fr: Effects of a Targeted Nutritional Intervention on Auditory-Visual Event-Related Potentials in South-Indian Infants: An Exploratory Analysis of a Cluster Randomized Trial.
auteurs: Kamath Akshata A, Kilpady Chaitra A, Tripathi Prashansa, Saji Aswathi, Sharma Sumit, Venugopal Rahul, Sasidharan Arun, Shivakumar Nirupama, Kurpad Anura V
resume: Background/Objectives: Inadequate macronutrient intake may affect neurodevelopment in early infancy. In India, government-supplied take-home rations (THRs) attempt to meet this gap but lack adequate fat and protein. This study evaluated the impact of a 3-month macronutrient modified-THR intervention on infant neurodevelopment using event-related potentials (ERPs). Methods: A two-group cluster randomized controlled trial (village clusters = 12/group; N = 67/group) enrolled healthy breastfed infants (6-9 months) in Karnataka, India. The intervention group received a milk-legume-based THR providing ~200 kcal/day (ML-THR, estimated protein:energy (PE) and fat:energy (FE) ratios: 12% and 45%) with the standard government THR (SG-THR, estimated PE and FE ratios: 7% and 4%), while controls received SG-THRs only. All mothers received education on infant and young child feeding practices, water sanitation and hygiene. Auditory, visual and attention processing ERPs were measured using a short, culturally adapted, infant-friendly paradigm. Linear mixed models evaluated intervention effects over time. Results: The intervention was associated with region-specific visual ERP changes: increased fractional latencies in anterior regions for face, nonface (500-750 ms); decreased fractional latencies in the central region for frequent (10-250 ms) and face (500-750 ms) and in the posterior region for frequent-rare difference (250-500 ms). The intervention group also demonstrated a reduced area under the curve for nonface stimuli (250-500 ms). No significant auditory or visual hemifield effects were observed. None of the observed effects remained significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Conclusions: The findings are exploratory and suggest the need to examine the effects of improved protein quality and fat content in THRs on visual-cortical processing in larger samples.

titre: The Early Nutrition Paradox in Preterm and Intrauterine Growth Restricted (IUGR) Infants: A Critical Review of the Developmental Programming Hypothesis and the Limits of Its Evidence.
titre_fr: The Early Nutrition Paradox in Preterm and Intrauterine Growth Restricted (IUGR) Infants: A Critical Review of the Developmental Programming Hypothesis and the Limits of Its Evidence.
auteurs: Riskin Arieh, Iofe Adir, Safadi Rasha Zoabi, Tal Naama, Gover Ayala
resume: Nutrition during early life may be an important determinant of long-term health. Preterm birth, affecting approximately 10% of deliveries worldwide, and intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) are major perinatal conditions. The Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD) hypothesis proposes that early nutritional and environmental exposures shape adult disease risk. This narrative review synthesizes epidemiological, cohort, animal, and interventional evidence on early nutrition and long-term outcomes in these infants. Rapid weight gain has been associated with later obesity and cardio-metabolic risk; however, this does not show that the tempo of gain, rather than attained size, carries the risk, and catch-up growth after preterm birth or growth restriction supports neurodevelopment. Preterm birth has been associated with a 53% higher risk of ischemic heart disease, whereas IUGR confers overlapping but distinct risks. Hypothesized mechanisms include epigenetic modification, structural organ deficits, hormonal reprogramming, gut-microbiome dysbiosis, and oxidative stress. Because the human evidence is almost entirely observational and vulnerable to confounding and to over-adjustment for attained body size, these associations should be read as hypotheses rather than established causal effects. Individualized, guideline-based and responsive feeding strategies, with support for mothers to provide their own milk, are needed to optimize immediate outcomes while limiting lifelong disease susceptibility.

titre: Disentangling Fat and Sugar in the Western Diet: Parental Consumption of a High-Fat Diet Alters Offspring Brain Development.
titre_fr: Disentangling Fat and Sugar in the Western Diet: Parental Consumption of a High-Fat Diet Alters Offspring Brain Development.
auteurs: Lee Gail, Wilk Karina, DeYoung Taylor, Chong Cheryl, McKnight Emma G W, Ayoub Tiffany, Fan Lloyd, Ellegood Jacob, Beauchamp Antoine, Foster Jane A, Zhang Tie-Yuan, Lerch Jason P, Palmert Mark R, Nieman Brian J
resume: Maternal consumption of the Western diet is a precursor for metabolic conditions such as obesity and is associated with increased offspring risk for neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs). It is not clear which component (i.e., high-fat or high-sugar) of the Western diet contributes to changes in offspring neurodevelopment. We used a mouse model of parental consumption of five different diets containing varying levels of fat and sugar to examine and compare their effects on offspring brain structure. Male and female offspring (avg n = 15/sex/diet) were assessed for differences in body weight and developmental milestone achievement, and their brains were imaged at postnatal day (P) 65 using magnetic resonance imaging to compare brain structure. Offspring of the high-fat-only and combined high-fat/high-sugar diet groups showed delayed righting reflex success and heavier weight at weaning. Brain structure differences were also observed in early adulthood (P65), with the pattern of change induced by high-fat/high-sugar diets similar to that observed in some autism mouse models. Parental high-fat-only and combined high-fat/high-sugar diets altered offspring brain structure, but the high-sugar-only diet did not. High fat consumption is likely a key driver of the observed offspring brain changes and is a modifiable risk factor for NDDs.

titre: Trimester-Specific Associations Between Maternal Fatty Acid Ratios and Cognitive and Executive Functioning in 4-Year-Old Children.
titre_fr: Trimester-Specific Associations Between Maternal Fatty Acid Ratios and Cognitive and Executive Functioning in 4-Year-Old Children.
auteurs: Kou Xiruo, Canals Josefa, Arija Victoria
resume: Purpose: Early prenatal fatty acid balance is vital for brain development, yet trimester-specific effects on long-term neurodevelopment remain unclear. This study examined associations between maternal omega-6/omega-3 (n-6/n-3) ratios in the first and third trimesters and child neurodevelopment at age four. Methods: In the ECLIPSES cohort (n = 223), maternal serum n-3 and n-6 fatty acids were measured at 12 and 36 gestational weeks. At age four, children's cognitive and executive function were assessed using the Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence (WPPSI), and the Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function (BRIEF)-Preschool Version, respectively. Multivariable regression models were adjusted for sociodemographic and lifestyle factors. Results: A higher n-6/n-3 ratio in the first trimester was significantly associated with poorer executive functioning, as reflected by higher BRIEF scores indicating greater difficulties in inhibition (b = 2.45, p = 0.002), working memory (b = 1.87, p = 0.030), planning/organization (b = 2.20, p = 0.004), and the Global Executive Composite (b = 1.96, p = 0.006). Higher first-trimester ratios were also associated with lower WPPSI working memory performance (b = -2.14, p = 0.013), while general cognitive abilities were largely unaffected. Conclusions: An elevated maternal n-6/n-3 ratio in early pregnancy is associated with poorer executive function in preschool children, whereas evidence linking these ratios to general cognition remains limited. These findings indicate that associations between fatty acid balance and executive function were mainly observed during the first trimester.

titre: Extracellular Vesicles in Pregnancy: From Maternal-Fetal Communication to Environmental Perturbation.
titre_fr: Extracellular Vesicles in Pregnancy: From Maternal-Fetal Communication to Environmental Perturbation.
auteurs: Affranchi Federica, Aloi Noemi, Cosentini Ilaria, Smeraldi Giulia, Colombo Paolo, Drago Gaspare, Ruggieri Silvia, Longo Valeria
resume: Pregnancy is a uniquely sensitive moment during which environmental exposures may have profound and long-lasting consequences for maternal health, placental function, and fetal development. A successful pregnancy depends on continuous molecular communication among maternal, placental, and fetal compartments. The disruption of these processes by environmental stressors may increase the risk of pregnancy complications, impaired neurodevelopment, and susceptibility to non-communicable diseases later in life. Pregnant women are exposed to dynamic mixtures of chemical, physical, occupational, behavioral, and social stressors from the air, diet, drinking water, consumer products, and residential or workplace environments. The pregnancy exposome framework integrates these external exposures with internal biological responses, including oxidative stress, inflammation, metabolic dysregulation, epigenetic alterations, and changes in circulating biomolecules. However, the mechanisms through which exposure-related signals are transmitted across the maternal-placental-fetal unit remain incompletely understood. Extracellular vesicles may be a key component of this communication network as they transfer protected molecular cargoes, including proteins, lipids, metabolites, and regulatory nucleic acids. Understanding how environmental exposures modify extracellular vesicle biogenesis, composition, and function may reveal mechanisms linking the pregnancy exposome to placental dysfunction, adverse pregnancy outcomes, fetal programming, and early biomarkers of biological effects. This review examines the role of extracellular vesicles in physiological maternal-fetal communication and critically summarizes current human and experimental evidence on how environmental exposures may affect EV characteristics and function during pregnancy, with particular attention to their potential involvement in placental dysfunction and adverse pregnancy outcomes.

titre: Long-Term Effects of Isoflurane Anesthesia and Surgery: Sex-Associated Neurological Dysfunction and Alterations in Circulating Extracellular Vesicles.
titre_fr: Long-Term Effects of Isoflurane Anesthesia and Surgery: Sex-Associated Neurological Dysfunction and Alterations in Circulating Extracellular Vesicles.
auteurs: Li Yun, Park Ruth, Krishnamachary Balaji, Lee Hangnoh, Lei Zhuofan, Li Hui, Wu Junfang
resume: Volatile anesthetics and surgery can trigger neuroinflammation and neurological dysfunction, but their long-term effects remain poorly understood. Young adult male and female C57BL/6 mice underwent 4 h of 2% isoflurane anesthesia combined with laparotomy (Iso/OP) or sham treatment. At 12 weeks, olfactory and cognitive functions were assessed, followed by RNA sequencing of olfactory bulbs and hippocampi and plasma extracellular vesicle (EV) profiling. EV-associated inflammatory bioactivity was evaluated by hippocampal injection into naïve male mice. Iso/OP induced olfactory deficits at 12 weeks, with greater impairment in females. Female mice also exhibited deficits in spatial working memory and associative learning, whereas males showed relatively preserved cognitive function. Transcriptomic analyses revealed sex-dependent alterations in pathways related to synaptic function, neurodevelopment, extracellular matrix remodeling, stress responses, and chemotaxis. Iso/OP reduced circulating EV abundance, particularly among 40-100 nm particles, and altered EV proteomic profiles. Exploratory analyses of pooled hippocampal tissues revealed distinct cytokine and chemokine profiles following injection of plasma EVs from the four donor groups. Collectively, these findings demonstrate sex-dependent neurological and molecular alterations persisting 12 weeks after Iso/OP, accompanied by changes in circulating EVs. The exploratory EV transfer findings warrant further investigation into the potential contribution of circulating EVs to brain inflammatory responses.

titre: Genetic Evidence Linking Gut-Brain Peptide Signaling to Anorexia Nervosa: Implications for Early Risk Detection.
titre_fr: Genetic Evidence Linking Gut-Brain Peptide Signaling to Anorexia Nervosa: Implications for Early Risk Detection.
auteurs: Zeng Xin, Chen Jie, Fu Yansong, Yang Keyi, Qin Hong
resume: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a severe psychiatric disorder with high mortality, yet its biological underpinnings remain unclear. Gut-brain peptides, which influence brain function through circulatory and vagal routes, have emerged as potential contributors to AN, though causal relationships remain unexplored. Given the unclear biological mechanisms and lack of biomarkers for AN, this study aims to explore the causal role of gut-brain peptides in AN development, in order to identify potential diagnostic or therapeutic targets. We applied Mendelian randomization (MR) to assess the causal effects of 12 gut-brain peptides on AN risk, using genome-wide association study (GWAS) data from populations of European ancestry. The inverse variance weighted (IVW) method was the primary analytic tool, supplemented with sensitivity analyses. Peptides showing associations with AN were also tested across five other psychiatric disorders: schizophrenia (SCZ), major depressive disorder (MDD), bipolar disorder (BD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)-were also explored. Elevated peptide YY (PYY) levels were causally linked to increased AN risk (OR = 1.07, 95% CI: 1.01-1.15, p = .035). No significant associations were found for the other peptides. Reverse MR showed that genetic liability to AN was associated with reduced levels of leptin and chromogranin A (CgA). These associations were not observed in the five other psychiatric disorders. This study identifies PYY as a potential causal factor in AN and highlights leptin and CgA as downstream biomarkers. These findings suggest gut-brain peptides may be uniquely involved in AN pathogenesis, offering targets for early detection and therapeutic intervention.

titre: Preliminary Investigation of Workplace Predictors of Job Turnover Among Autistic Adults: A 12-Month Follow-Up Study.
titre_fr: Preliminary Investigation of Workplace Predictors of Job Turnover Among Autistic Adults: A 12-Month Follow-Up Study.
auteurs: Taylor Julie Lounds, Moser Carly, Durrani Eman, Vogus Timothy J, Smith DaWalt Leann
revue: Autism : the international journal of research and practice
resume: Though the difficulties faced by autistic adults in obtaining employment are well-documented, little is known about job retention in this group. The present study fills this gap by examining the frequency of job turnover over 12 months for autistic adults with community employment and investigating work- and workplace-related predictors of turnover. Two waves of data, separated by 12 months, were collected from 83 autistic adults as part of a larger longitudinal study. Information about current community employment and changes in employment since Wave 1 was collected via interview. Surveys at Wave 1 included measures of perceived workplace climate and job satisfaction. Bivariate logistic regression models were used to examine whether job satisfaction, perceived workplace climate, or structural aspects of jobs (hours, pay) at Wave 1 predicted turnover. Just over one-third (37%) of participants experienced turnover in their primary job during this period. A less positive workplace climate and lower satisfaction with pay and opportunities for promotion predicted a higher likelihood of turnover. Results suggest that a supportive workplace climate, as well as pay and opportunities for promotion that are satisfying to the autistic adult, may be key factors for enhancing job stability.Lay AbstractWhy was the study done? Many studies have focused on understanding how to help autistic adults get jobs. But keeping those jobs can be very hard for autistic adults. We know little about how to help autistic adults keep jobs. This study tested aspects of jobs that might predict whether the autistic adult is still at their job 1 year later.What did the researchers do? Researchers interviewed 83 autistic adults twice, 1 year apart. Researchers asked about the jobs that autistic adults were working at each time point. They also used a questionnaire to ask about adults' satisfaction with their jobs and how they felt about their workplace environment.What did the researchers find? About one-third of autistic adults left their main job during the 1-year period. Autistic adults who felt that their workplace environment was less supportive, or who were less satisfied with their pay or their opportunities to get higher positions, were more likely to leave their job.What do the findings mean? Our findings tell us about the types of workplaces that might support autistic adults in keeping their jobs, including workplaces that are supportive and accepting, and provide pay and opportunities for moving into higher positions that are in line with the adult's preferences.

titre: Data Sharing in Autism Research: Case Studies From the United States and the United Kingdom and Recommendations for Practice.
titre_fr: Data Sharing in Autism Research: Case Studies From the United States and the United Kingdom and Recommendations for Practice.
auteurs: Grant Aimee, Ellis Rebecca, Axbey Harriet, Nisa Ami, Waldock Krysia Emily, Brown Amy, McDonald Katherine E, Beck Kelly B, Sabatello Maya, Moura Ian, Kirby Anne V, Rutenberg Elizabeth, Breitenfeldt Kaitlyn E, Williams Kathryn, Craine Monique, Wilkins Abigail, Caemawr Selena, Holloway Willow, Sinfield Madeleine, Ribbons-Steen Kay, Raymaker Dora M, Kripke-Ludwig Rachel, Baker-Ericzén Mary, Vera Joseph, Nicolaidis Christina
revue: Autism : the international journal of research and practice
resume: Data sharing has become common in Autism research. In the context of a history of eugenics, additional risks are present, including re-identification, misinterpretation and deficit-framing of Autism. We, a group of community members and researchers, aimed to (a) describe our 'opt-in' data-sharing approach in two Community-Based Participatory Research studies based in the United States (AASPIRE Outcomes Project) and the United Kingdom (Autism from Menstruation to Menopause; AM2M), (b) report on how many people opted to data share and (c) co-develop recommendations for ethical data sharing in Autism research. In the AASPIRE Outcomes Project, 680 of 870 (78.2%) participants opted to share quantitative survey data, with no differences by demographic, disability, or health characteristics. In AM2M, 36 of 100 (36.0%) participants opted to share longitudinal qualitative data, with significant variation when controlling for family-wise error rate by menopause status (p = .007). We provide recommendations for ethical data sharing in Autism research, directed at governments, policy makers, research funders, data repositories, ethics boards and researchers. We favour approaches that centre autonomy and dignity, including, 'opt-in' data-sharing consent models and Autistic community participation. We hope that these recommendations will balance data-sharing benefits with strong protections for Autistic research participants.Lay AbstractData sharing is when people's information from a study are anonymised (names taken out) and shared in an online library. Other researchers can use this data to answer new research questions at reduced cost.Some funders say researchers must share data. However, some Autistic people worry this could be bad for Autistic people. One solution is letting research participants decide if they want to share their answers. This is called 'opt-in' data sharing.We are a neurodiverse group of Autism researchers and community members. We had three goals:1. Share how we handled data sharing in studies in the United States and the United Kingdom;2. Say how many people agreed to data share3. Make recommendations for ethical data sharing in Autism research.We had concerns about data sharing, including not keeping participants' identities private and researchers doing studies that were dehumanising or used deficit views of Autism. For this reason, the U.S. study decided not to share interview data, and both studies used separate data-sharing information and consent forms after people had decided to take part in the study.In our U.S.-based survey study, most people (680 of 870 or 78%) decided to data share their survey data. There were not many differences between people who did or did not decide to share their data. In our U.K.-based interview study, one third (36.0%) of 100 participants decided to share their interview data. Menopausal participants shared less often.We developed best-practice recommendations for Autism research data sharing. We make suggestions for governments, research funders, data repositories, ethics boards and researchers. We recommend using 'opt-in' consent for data sharing. We also think Autistic adults should be involved in deciding if new research that uses shared data is good for the Autistic community.We hope these recommendations will provide stronger protections for Autistic research participants.

titre: Everyday Sensory Experiences of Autistic University Students in Australia: An Experience Sampling Approach.
titre_fr: Everyday Sensory Experiences of Autistic University Students in Australia: An Experience Sampling Approach.
auteurs: Dwyer Patrick, Broadbent Laura T, Bower Max, Curtis Sarah, Hariz Caden, Plozza Keira, Briese Elizabeth, Unwin Katy
revue: Autism : the international journal of research and practice
resume: Sensory differences and discomfort are significant on-campus barriers for many autistic postsecondary students, but we know relatively little about what makes sensory environments accessible or inaccessible for autistic students. In this study, 19 autistic university students in Australia answered experience sampling questions thrice daily for 2 weeks. Quantitative sensory comfort ratings were significantly poorer when participants reported states of greater anxiety, irritability, emotional reactivity and exhaustion. Participants also reported more quantitative sensory discomfort when open-ended answers described feeling tired/exhausted, anxious or stressed/overwhelmed, rather than feeling relaxed/good. Our study cannot resolve the causality of these relationships. Notably, however, between-person trait differences in anxiety, irritability and exhaustion were not statistically related to sensory comfort. Qualitative-quantitative triangulation suggested that participants experienced less sensory comfort: in open-access spaces (notably, on campus, travelling and shopping) compared to closed-access spaces (notably, at home); to high-intensity (e.g., loud) than low-intensity (e.g., quiet) or non-notable stimulation; to most sounds over visual, feel and taste stimuli; to people-related sounds than touch sensations; and to crowds over environments with fewer people. These findings suggest sensory environments systematically shape many autistic people's everyday experiences and thus that we should modify these environments to be more accessible and inclusive.

titre: Non-invasive physiotherapy interventions for autistic children and adolescents using the F-words Lens Tool: A scoping review.
titre_fr: Non-invasive physiotherapy interventions for autistic children and adolescents using the F-words Lens Tool: A scoping review.
auteurs: Soares Esther G, Leite Hércules R, de Sousa Junior Ricardo R, Félix Jean B, de Lima Arthur Felipe B, Ferreira Lidiane F B, Netto Reinaldo da C P, Longo Egmar, Souto Deisiane O
resume: To map non-invasive physiotherapy interventions for individuals with autism spectrum disorder, using the F-words Lens Tool to summarize the main components of these interventions. We searched PubMed, Web of Science, PEDro, Embase, the Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Scopus for studies published between 2001 and 2026 involving autistic children and adolescents. Intervention components were analysed using the Rehabilitation Treatment Specification System and linked to the F-words through the F-words Lens Tool framework. The review was co-developed with patient and public involvement. Forty-eight studies were included. Most interventions were delivered by physiotherapists (71%), whereas 29% were interdisciplinary. Twenty-eight distinct interventions were identified, with ingredients covering five F-words domains: Functioning (e.g. structured and repetitive motor task practice; 67.96%); Fitness (e.g. aerobic and resistance exercises; 60.7%); Friends (e.g. group activities and facilitation of social interaction; 35.71%), Family (e.g. parent training and adaptation of routines; 20.8%); and Fun (e.g. meaningful and motivating activities; 14.3%). No components related to the Future domain were identified. Interventions mainly focused on functioning and fitness, with limited attention to the Future domain. The F-words Lens Tool helped identify important gaps and support more comprehensive, person-centred approaches.

Twenty-eight distinct interventions were identified, with ingredients covering five F-words domains: Functioning (e.g. structured and repetitive motor task practice; 67.96%); Fitness (e.g. aerobic and resistance exercises; 60.7%); Friends (e.g. group activities and facilitation of social interaction; 35.71%), Family (e.g. parent training and adaptation of routines; 20.8%); and Fun (e.g. meaningful and motivating activities; 14.3%). No components related to the Future domain were identified. Interventions mainly focused on functioning and fitness, with limited attention to the Future domain. The F-words Lens Tool helped identify important gaps and support more comprehensive, person-centred approaches.

titre: Heterogeneous Encoding Patterns of Dynamic Audiovisual Social Stimuli in Autism Spectrum Disorder (Heterogeneous Encoding Patterns in Autism).
titre_fr: Heterogeneous Encoding Patterns of Dynamic Audiovisual Social Stimuli in Autism Spectrum Disorder (Heterogeneous Encoding Patterns in Autism).
auteurs: Van De Water Avery L, Byrge Lisa, Kennedy Daniel P, Kliemann Dorit, Traer James A
revue: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
resume: The neural basis of social difficulties in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) remains uncertain. Prior studies typically used static stimuli or reduced complex stimuli to only a few dimensions, obscuring real-world complexity. Here, we used videos with social content to engage brain networks and trained encoding models to predict brain activity from high-dimensional audio, visual, and more abstract socially relevant features (e.g., valence). We hypothesized that brain activity in autistic adults would be less accurately predicted and more heterogeneous within and across individuals than in neurotypical (NT) participants, particularly for socially relevant features. Participants [48 ASD (13 female), 90 NT (25 female)] viewed six videos (5-20 min). Brain activity was measured using fMRI. Cross-validated encoding models were assessed on prediction accuracy, variance, and pattern similarity. Brain activity was predicted significantly above chance across brain networks and videos with striking consistency between groups. Auditory and language networks were most accurately predicted. Within-participant predictions were equally variable between groups; however, autistic participants exhibited lower within-group encoding pattern similarity than NT participants and greater across-group than within-group similarity. Analyses using only socially relevant features showed the largest across-group differences in encoding pattern similarity. The novel application of encoding models to multiple videos in ASD suggests greater heterogeneity in neural representations of social information in ASD. Although group-averaged encoding accuracies were comparable across groups, ASD participants showed more heterogeneous regional encoding patterns. These idiosyncratic patterns underscore the need to incorporate individual variation in brain representations when developing translational neuroimaging approaches in autism.Significance statement Individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) experience difficulties in social communication and interaction, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we present a novel application of encoding models to neuroimaging in ASD. Neural representations of dynamic and complex social information were more heterogeneous across autistic as compared with neurotypical individuals while encoding model prediction accuracy was similar for population averages across groups. Effects were robust across six videos and spatial scales. Variability in neural representation across individuals, rather than systemic population differences, may thus be associated with atypical brain function in complex social information processing in autism. The findings highlight the importance of accounting for individual variability when studying the neurobiology of autism and developing translational neuroimaging approaches.

titre: Patterns of Intravenous Buprenorphine-Naloxone Misuse: Psychiatric Morbidity, Risk Behaviours, Diversion, and Serological Findings.
titre_fr: Patterns of Intravenous Buprenorphine-Naloxone Misuse: Psychiatric Morbidity, Risk Behaviours, Diversion, and Serological Findings.
auteurs: Khanam Aaliya, Raj Rajnish, Khare Vaibhav Kumar, Gidwani Sunny, Haq Inaamul, Bhat Fazle Roub, Wani Zaid Ahmad, Rather Yasir Hassan
resume: Intravenous misuse of buprenorphine-naloxone (BPNX) is a growing concern for patients with opioid use disorder (OUD). However, data on psychiatric comorbidities, patterns of diversion, and the burden of infectious diseases among individuals who inject BPNX in India remain limited. This study aimed to assess the clinical profile, diversion patterns, and seroprevalence among these patients. Seventy-three patients with a diagnosis of OUD injecting BPNX, were recruited for this study. Sociodemographic and clinical variables, diversion patterns, high-risk behaviors, and overdose history were assessed using a semi-structured proforma. Triple serology testing for HIV, HBV, and HCV was conducted, and relevant statistical analyses were performed. The participants were predominantly young men with a mean age of 25.9 ± 6.05 years. Psychiatric comorbidity was present in 67.1% of participants, and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) was the most common diagnosis. HCV seropositivity was found in 68.5% and HCV RNA in 52.05%. Most participants used both prescription and diverted BPNX to avoid withdrawal symptoms. High-frequency misuse was significantly linked to longer opioid dependence and needle sharing. The misuse of intravenous BPNX was linked to significant psychiatric comorbidity, unsafe injection practices, and a high burden of infectious diseases. The persistence of diversion despite the BPNX combination formulation suggests the current naloxone dose ratio may not be effective as a deterrent. Urgent integrated addiction, psychiatric, and harm-reduction services are needed.

titre: Autistic traits among doctors seeking mental health support.
titre_fr: Autistic traits among doctors seeking mental health support.
auteurs: Abeyratne L, Courtenay K, Al-Najjar Z, Shaw S C K, Odiaka V, Doherty M, Perera B
resume: Neurodevelopmental differences are increasingly recognised in understanding mental health difficulties. However, autism among doctors experiencing mental health problems remains underexplored. To assess the prevalence of screening positive for autism among doctors seeking mental health support and examine associations with demographic characteristics, medical speciality, co-occurring mental health difficulties, and neurodevelopmental differences. We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of self-reported data from doctors accessing National Health Service Practitioner Health between April and July 2024. The Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ-10) screened for autism alongside validated measures of depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), psychological distress (CORE-10), and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) (ASRS-6). Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were used to assess associations with demographic, clinical, and speciality variables. Of the 946 doctors included, 14% screened positive for autism using the AQ-10. Positive screening was associated with male sex (odds ratio [OR]: 1.71, confidence interval [CI]: 1.14, 2.55), age 22-29 (OR: 1.87, CI: 1.06, 3.30), and working in psychiatry (OR: 2.22, CI: 1.07, 4.63). No other specialty was significantly associated with screening positive for autism. Those who screened positive for autism had significantly higher odds of also screening positive for ADHD (OR 2.22, CI: 1.50, 3.28). Nearly one in seven doctors screening positive for autism highlights the need for considering the role of neurodevelopmental differences in this professional group. This may help to adapt assessments and interventions to accommodate the neurodivergent needs of the workforce.

titre: Reduced Cytokine Production in a CYFIP1-Mediated Model of Autism Spectrum Disorder.
titre_fr: Reduced Cytokine Production in a CYFIP1-Mediated Model of Autism Spectrum Disorder.
auteurs: Kolomina E S, Kuzmina D M, Chernova M A, Vasilyeva E A, Mukhina I V
revue: Bulletin of experimental biology and medicine
resume: CYFIP1 (Cytoplasmic FMR1 Interacting Protein 1) is a key component of the regulatory complex controlling actin polymerization, which is critically important for neuronal morphogenesis, synapse formation, and the maintenance of synaptic plasticity. Reduced CYFIP1 gene expression is associated with autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia, epilepsy, and developmental delay. Cyfip1 haploinsufficient (Cyfip1<sup>+/-</sup>) mice demonstrate not only behavioral deficiency, but also diminished production of cytokines, key regulators of the immune response. This CYFIP1-dependent imbalance of immune system regulators may result in an inadequate response to proinflammatory stimuli in patients with neuropsychiatric symptoms. This phenomenon should be taken into account when developing therapeutic strategies for these patients.

titre: Dietary Clostridium butyricum NCU-02 and Its Postbiotic Butyrate Ameliorate Autism Spectrum Disorder-like Symptoms: Involvement of Hippocampal Oxidative Stress Modulation.
titre_fr: Dietary Clostridium butyricum NCU-02 and Its Postbiotic Butyrate Ameliorate Autism Spectrum Disorder-like Symptoms: Involvement of Hippocampal Oxidative Stress Modulation.
auteurs: Zeng Kangtai, Wu Qiuyu, Wang Liye, Liu Chengrui, Li Mengqian, Chen Tingtao, Luo Jie
resume: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition closely linked to gut microbiota dysbiosis and gut-brain axis dysfunction, yet effective dietary interventions remain limited. This study evaluated the therapeutic potential of Clostridium butyricum NCU-02, a probiotic candidate, and its sterile supernatant in a valproic acid (VPA)-induced mouse model of ASD, with emphasis on their postbiotic properties. Both treatments significantly ameliorated core ASD-like behaviors, attenuating repetitive marble-burying by over 35% and restoring social novelty preference to near-control levels (p < 0.05 for both). These interventions were associated with improved intestinal barrier integrity, upregulated tight junction proteins (ZO-1 and occludin), and suppressed colonic and hippocampal pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α). Metabolomics profiling identified butyrate as a key differential metabolite, with butyrate levels elevated by approximately 1.3- to 2.5-fold following interventions (all p < 0.05 vs. M group). Correlation analyses further linked butyrate elevation to activation of the hippocampal GPR109A/AMPK/Nrf2 pathway and reduction of oxidative stress markers. Collectively, these findings suggest that C. butyricum NCU-02 and its sterile supernatant are associated with protective effects against ASD-like symptoms, and that the postbiotic metabolite butyrate may contribute to these benefits through dual modulation of gut homeostasis and neuroprotective signaling. A sodium-butyrate comparison group reproduced several of these effects, indicating that exogenous butyrate is sufficient to reproduce several of these effects, although the present design does not establish butyrate as a necessary mediator for the live-strain effects. These findings position butyrate, and butyrate-producing probiotics, as promising candidates for dietary intervention in neurodevelopmental disorders.

titre: Neurobehavioral Assessment of ADHD and Anxiety Co-occurrence in Pediatric Populations.
titre_fr: Neurobehavioral Assessment of ADHD and Anxiety Co-occurrence in Pediatric Populations.
auteurs: Sabaghypour Saied, Farkhondeh Tale Navi Farhad, Radaee Maryam, Zadehahmad Sabzi Amid, Masoudi Mahshad, Davoodabadi Samane, Shakibaei Fereshteh
resume: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is frequently comorbid with anxiety, a condition that complicates diagnosis and treatment. Stimulant medications used to treat ADHD may exacerbate anxiety in some children, although this is not a consistent effect. This study investigates Alpha Peak Frequency (APF) as a potential neurophysiological marker, alongside Theta/Beta Ratio (TBR) and Sensorimotor Rhythm (SMR), to compare children with ADHD alone (ADHD group) and those with ADHD and comorbid anxiety (COM group) using electrophysiological and behavioral assessments. We assessed 98 children (8-16 years, M = 10.1, SD = 2.25) diagnosed with ADHD based on DSM-5 criteria, divided into ADHD (n = 46) and COM (n = 52) groups. Behavioral measures included the Conners' Parent Rating Scale-Revised (CPRS-R) and the Spence Children's Anxiety Scale (SCAS). EEG data were analyzed to compare APF, TBR, and SMR across frontal, central, and occipital regions. The COM group exhibited significantly higher SCAS anxiety scores but no significant differences in ADHD symptom severity compared to the ADHD group. EEG analysis revealed an overall reduction in APF in the COM group compared to the ADHD group, with multiplicity-adjusted post hoc comparisons confirming significantly lower APF at the central and occipital electrodes. Additionally, compared to the ADHD group, the COM group showed reduced SMR at the central site, lower TBR in the occipital region, and higher occipital beta activity. APF, TBR, and SMR differed between children with ADHD and COM groups. These group differences require replication, and their diagnostic or treatment-related relevance remains to be established.

titre: Nicotinic Cholinergic Signaling in Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Secondary Analysis of Receptor Abnormalities and Pharmacological Responses.
titre_fr: Nicotinic Cholinergic Signaling in Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Secondary Analysis of Receptor Abnormalities and Pharmacological Responses.
auteurs: Bjørklund Geir, Gurgas Leonard, Hangan Tony
resume: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) abnormalities and pharmacological responses have been reported in autism spectrum disorder (ASD), but their relationships across human and experimental studies remain unclear. This descriptive secondary analysis used a focused nonsystematic search to select 21 original reports: five human postmortem or molecular, six human pharmacological, and ten experimental ASD-model reports. Comparisons addressed receptor binding, expression and function, percentage differences from published means, exposure-response patterns, antagonist experiments, and compatibility across evidence levels. Human postmortem findings repeatedly showed reduced high-affinity binding and α4/β2-related expression. However, four reports arose from a connected research program, and some binding data were reused. α7 findings varied by region and measurement. Experimental findings differed by model, developmental stage, sex, compound, and outcome. The eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E (eIF4E) study identified impaired β2-containing receptor function without establishing α4β2 identity. α7-related pharmacological effects and antagonist evidence were outcome-specific; valproate-exposed rats showed both positive and null findings. Nicotine and maternal immune activation experiments provided complementary neuroimmune evidence. Human intervention studies reported preliminary physiological, behavioral, or neurocognitive responses without establishing efficacy. The selected findings support nicotinic pathway involvement, although postmortem dependence and experimental heterogeneity limit generalization. They do not establish a uniform receptor deficit, a shared mechanism across species, or clinical benefit.

titre: When extended-release methylphenidate underperforms: three children with ADHD and gastrointestinal disease.
titre_fr: When extended-release methylphenidate underperforms: three children with ADHD and gastrointestinal disease.
auteurs: Caci Hervé
resume: Methylphenidate (MPH) is the first-line pharmacological treatment for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children, available in immediate-release (IR) and extended-release (ER) formulations with distinct release profiles. Whether gastrointestinal pathology might selectively affect one or the other has received little clinical attention. We here report three patients with ADHD followed in a single paediatric centre, each with a gastrointestinal disease affecting either absorption (cystic fibrosis) or motility (idiopathic gastroparesis, and gastroparesis in a child with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1 A). In all three, IR-MPH doses produced clearer per-dose responses than ER-MPH at some stage of follow-up; multiple daily IR-MPH doses achieved successful overall management in Cases 1 and 2, whereas Case 3 required a combined ER-IR regimen due to unmanageable peak-and-trough fluctuations under IR monotherapy. In the cystic fibrosis case, the introduction of CFTR-modulator triple therapy was followed, after a delay, by a within-patient reversal of the IR/ER preference. These observations raise the hypothesis that gastrointestinal disorders affecting upper gastrointestinal transit or absorption may alter the relative clinical performance of different MPH formulations, which deserves explicit consideration when selecting a formulation.

titre: Substantiation, Foster Care Entry, and Exit Type Among Children With Autism and Intellectual Disability: A Linked Child Welfare and Medicaid Study.
titre_fr: Substantiation, Foster Care Entry, and Exit Type Among Children With Autism and Intellectual Disability: A Linked Child Welfare and Medicaid Study.
auteurs: Anderson Kristy A, Cheatham Leah P, Radey Melissa, Rast Jessica E, Font Sarah
revue: Autism research : official journal of the International Society for Autism Research
resume: Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID) are disproportionately involved in child protective services (CPS). Whether these differences are concentrated at particular CPS decision points remains unclear. This study examined decision-point disparities among children with ASD-only (N = 20,657), ID-only (N = 2419), co-occurring ASD and ID (ASD + ID; N = 2168), and neither diagnosis (N = 599,100). Using linked child welfare and Medicaid data from Florida (2016-2021), we estimated adjusted odds of substantiation among Medicaid-observed children with at least one CPS report and of foster care entry among those with a substantiated report and modeled type of foster care exit (reunification, adoption, guardianship, or aging out) among children who exited custody. Diagnostic-group differences were larger for substantiation than for foster care entry. Children with ID-only and ASD + ID had higher adjusted odds of substantiated maltreatment than children with no ASD/ID, whereas the estimate for children with ASD-only was only slightly elevated. No substantively meaningful diagnostic-group differences in foster care entry were observed, although these estimates do not establish equivalence. After adjustment, children with ID-only and ASD + ID were more likely to age out, and children with ASD + ID were substantially less likely to exit through guardianship. Because foster care placement confers Medicaid eligibility, the substantiated sample may overrepresent removed children and attenuate differences at foster care entry. These analyses identify where diagnostic-group differences occur but cannot determine why. Aggregate measures of disability and of foster care exit obscure both elevated substantiation and nonpermanent exits among children with ID.

titre: Research progress on developmental characteristics and clinical intervention of restricted and repetitive interests/behaviors in autism spectrum disorder across the lifespan: a narrative review.
titre_fr: Research progress on developmental characteristics and clinical intervention of restricted and repetitive interests/behaviors in autism spectrum disorder across the lifespan: a narrative review.
auteurs: Zhou Lei, Dai Ying
resume: Restricted and repetitive interests/behaviors (RRBs) are a core symptom domain of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), with a significant impact on social interaction, learning, and overall functioning of autistic individuals. Clinical features of RRBs in ASD encompass repetitive sensorimotor (RSM) behaviors and insistence on sameness (IS). Taking a lifespan approach, this narrative review synthesizes current understanding of the neurobiological and psychological mechanisms associated with RRBs, together with their clinical manifestations during each developmental phase, and discusses recent advances in clinical interventions. Importantly, the available evidence is not distributed evenly across the lifespan: RRBs have been studied far more extensively in early childhood, whereas evidence concerning middle-aged and older autistic adults remains very limited. This review therefore does not imply that the evidence base is equally strong at every life stage. It aims to provide a practical clinical reference for professionals in pediatrics, rehabilitation medicine, and related fields.

Importantly, the available evidence is not distributed evenly across the lifespan: RRBs have been studied far more extensively in early childhood, whereas evidence concerning middle-aged and older autistic adults remains very limited. This review therefore does not imply that the evidence base is equally strong at every life stage. It aims to provide a practical clinical reference for professionals in pediatrics, rehabilitation medicine, and related fields.

titre: A progenitor with immature Bergmann glia-like characteristics in the developing cerebellar cortex.
titre_fr: A progenitor with immature Bergmann glia-like characteristics in the developing cerebellar cortex.
auteurs: Sawada Kazuhiko
resume: The cerebellum is an ancient brain component, conserved across mammalian species, that has classically played roles in regulating muscle tone, limb coordination, and equilibrium, as well as in non-motor functions, such as language, cognition, and emotion. Recently, we reported Nestin-expressing cells in the cerebellar cortex of ferret neonates that showed a proliferative potency defined by proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) immunostaining. We called these cells "internal granular progenitor (IGP)." IGPs were found to be abundant in the internal granular layer adjacent to the Purkinje cell layer and extended GFAP-immunopositive radials progressed through the molecular and external granular layers, forming an immature Bergmann glia-like morphology. The tracking of BrdU-labeling revealed that IGPs differentiated into granular neurons, Bergmann glia, and/or astrocytes. As such, we propose that IGPs may be neural progenitors with an immature Bergmann glia-like morphology that appear in the developing cerebellar cortex, and could serve as another source of granular neurons distinct from external granular progenitors. Further research on IGPs is expected to provide new perspectives for the future investigation of cerebellar corticohistogensis, particularly the difference between motor and non-motor cerebellar regions, and how the abnormal development of IGPs relates to neurodevelopmental disorders associated with non-motor cerebellar function, such as autism spectrum disorder.

titre: Exploring the feasibility and acceptability of sensory-adapted menus for adolescents with autism spectrum disorder in a school canteen: the AUT-MENU pilot study.
titre_fr: Exploring the feasibility and acceptability of sensory-adapted menus for adolescents with autism spectrum disorder in a school canteen: the AUT-MENU pilot study.
auteurs: Ruggeri Stefania, Antonazzi Francesca, Croci Ileana, Scalvedi Maria Luisa, Rocchi Benedetta, Conti Maria Vittoria, Breda Chiara, Zambon Ilaria, Basilico Sara, Cena Hellas, Marconi Emanuele
resume: Food Selectivity (FS) is highly prevalent among adolescents with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and may contribute to unbalanced dietary patterns and adverse nutritional outcomes. This pilot study assessed the feasibility and acceptability of sensory-adapted menus nutritionally planned in accordance with Italian dietary recommendations and Mediterranean dietary principles in a school canteen for adolescents with ASD. Eleven adolescents with ASD (14-20 years) participated in a two-phase pilot study consisting of an observational phase (T0) followed by a multicomponent intervention (T1) combining sensory-based menu modifications with changes in mealtime organisation. Sociodemographic and clinical characteristics were collected at baseline. Feeding Problems (FP) and adherence to the Mediterranean Diet (MD) were assessed pre- and post-intervention. Food consumption was assessed using the Pictorial Dietary Assessment Tool (PDAT). Analyses were primarily descriptive and exploratory. Descriptive changes in food acceptance varied by dish type. Consumption was higher at T1 for selected first courses and fish-based dishes whereas fruit acceptance was lower. Descriptive changes in mealtime-related behaviors were also observed, including greater peer interaction and less frequent excessive smartphone use. The observed changes in food acceptance, FS, dietary habits, and mealtime-related behavior represent preliminary exploratory findings and should not be interpreted as evidence of intervention effectiveness. Larger controlled intervention studies are needed to investigate the potential of school canteen environments to address food selectivity and support mealtime-related social behaviors among children and adolescents with ASD. https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06266377, identifier NCT06266377.

titre: Traditional and religious treatments administered to children with autism spectrum disorder in South Africa: a qualitative study of practices, composition and risk.
titre_fr: Traditional and religious treatments administered to children with autism spectrum disorder in South Africa: a qualitative study of practices, composition and risk.
auteurs: Simelane Ayanda, Mapaling Curwyn
resume: The appraisal of treatments for autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has largely focused on interventions delivered within formal healthcare systems, particularly in high-income settings. In South Africa, children with ASD may receive concurrent care from hospitals, traditional health practitioners and religious leaders, yet the practices administered outside formal healthcare remain poorly documented. This study aimed to identify these practices and interpret their potential risks in relation to published evidence of harm. A qualitative study was conducted at a public tertiary hospital in Soweto, Johannesburg. Semi-structured interviews were undertaken with 24 parents and caregivers and 10 hospital clinicians, alongside two focus groups involving traditional health practitioners and religious leaders, respectively. As practitioner participants did not recognise the term autism, they were briefed on its DSM-5 features before discussing practices previously administered to children presenting with similar characteristics. Their accounts therefore did not necessarily concern children with confirmed ASD diagnoses. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, followed by deductive recoding of reported practices into a route-of-administration taxonomy. Twenty-five distinct practices were identified. All children in the sample had received at least one intervention outside formal healthcare, with most receiving several alongside hospital treatment. Ingested and rectally administered preparations presented particular safety concerns because their constituents were undisclosed, dosing relied on clinical impression and paediatric formulations were unavailable. Neither caregivers nor clinicians could identify the substances administered, while practitioners declined to disclose their composition. Practitioners categorised ASD-related presentations within a broader conception of insanity, and one non-clinician proposed cutting tissue beneath a child's tongue to facilitate speech. Reported benefits, including explanatory frameworks, family connectedness and sustained hope, related primarily to caregivers' experiences rather than documented therapeutic improvements in children. The findings identify potentially harmful and insufficiently documented interventions administered alongside formal ASD care. Their safety cannot be adequately assessed without information about their constituents and administration. Route-based risk triage, non-punitive disclosure during clinical consultations and protected constituent disclosure are recommended. As the study was conducted at a single urban tertiary hospital, its findings are context-specific and should not be generalised beyond the setting investigated.

titre: Mental health staff perspectives on intellectual disability and autism: A cross-sectional survey.
titre_fr: Mental health staff perspectives on intellectual disability and autism: A cross-sectional survey.
auteurs: Franklin Catherine, Giesberts Amy, Brooker Katie, Trollor Julian N, Ware Robert S, Heffernan Edward
revue: Australasian psychiatry : bulletin of Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists
resume: BackgroundAutistic individuals and individuals with intellectual disability experience persistent inequities in mental health care, partly due to gaps in workforce capability.AimsTo assess knowledge, attitudes and self-efficacy of mainstream mental health staff regarding intellectual disability and autism, and to identify perceptions of barriers and potential improvements for care.MethodsA cross-sectional survey was conducted across three publicly funded mental health services from August 2022 to August 2023. Measures included the HK-IDA knowledge scale, the Classical and Modern Prejudice Scale and the AASPIRE self-efficacy scale. Open-ended responses were analysed using content analysis.ResultsKnowledge scores were moderate (M = 9.4/15; SD = 2.9). Attitudes were generally positive (Modern Prejudice totals: intellectual disability M = 19.5/44, SD = 4.3; autism M = 20.6/44, SD = 4.0). Self-efficacy was low-moderate (intellectual disability M = 15.6/35, SD = 8.5; autism M = 16.6/35, SD = 8.9) and was highest among medical staff and lowest among non-clinical staff. In adjusted models, profession and prior training predicted higher self-efficacy, whereas knowledge independently predicted lower prejudice but not self-efficacy.ConclusionMental health staff report reasonable knowledge but limited confidence in working with individuals with intellectual disability and autistic individuals. Knowledge relates to attitudes, while confidence appears to depend on applied, experiential learning. Workforce development should prioritise skills-based, experiential training that is applicable to all staff groups.
